subtopic: POSSIBLE CLOSING OF EDMONTON COAL MINES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. D. C. ABBOTT (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: POSSIBLE CLOSING OF EDMONTON COAL MINES
speechtext:
On Friday last, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) quoted an item appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of March 16, as follows:
Edmonton coal mines will dismiss 250 employees March 23 and the pits will close March 31 unless the federal government subsidy of 50 cents a ton is continued, mine officials said here to-day.
The hon. member asked whether the subsidy of 50 cents per ton would be continued on coal so that these mines in Alberta will continue to operate. There is no subsidy paid to any mine in Canada on a flat basis of 50 cents per ton. Therefore, I assume that the hon. member was speaking about the price increase which was authorized under wartime prices and trade board administrator's order No. A-1008 of December 1, 1943. The price increases authorized under this order were made to compensate the mine operators for the increased wages they were instructed to pay their men by the regional war labour board under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice O'Connor of Edmonton.
The authorized increase on Edmonton coal was 65 cents per ton on lump, egg and domestic mine run. It was 50 cents on regular mine

War Appropriation-Supplies
run coal, 25 cents per ton on stoker, nut and pea slack, and 10 cents on slack. The 65 cent increase has to be reduced to 50 cents as of April 1; the 50 cent increase of mine run has to be reduced to 40 cents as of April 1. No reductions have been ordered on the other sizes.

In making my report to the house on the production programme in this, the fifth year of the war, I would like to cite the following significant figures: The total dollar value of the contracts awarded by the Department of Munitions and Supply and its predecessors, the defence purchasing commission and the war supplies board, is now approximately 9 billion 450 million dollars. Capital expenditures by the government for war production purposes are in excess of 850 million dollars. I have had prepared a statement showing such capital expenditures up to December 31, 1943. I would ask that this be printed as a supplement to the votes and proceedings for the information of the members during the discussion of the munitions programme. It is important to note that the assets created by the government's capital expenditure, whether they be land, buildings or equipment, have remained in the ownership of the crown. The estimated total value of war production, including the value of deliveries on orders placed abroad, war construction and capital expenditures, in the fiscal year 1943-44, is 3 billion 435 million dollars, as compared with 2 billion 900 million dollars in the fiscal year 1942-43. We estimate that the number of persons engaged in direct and indirect war employment is in excess of a million, of whom about 800,000 are actually engaged in manufacturing war equipment. The fourth quarter of 1943 saw the highest level of employment in the history of Canada.
It is interesting to note that the value of war production proper, excluding capital expenditures, construction projects, and orders placed abroad, showed an increase of more than 150 per cent in 1942 over 1941, and an increase of about 35 per cent in 1943 over 1942. The value of war production proper for 1944 will show an increase of approximately 3 per cent over 1943. However, we are still in the early months of 1944, and our experience in the past indicates that the programme is usually stepped up beyond what we plan in the early part of the year. If we include capital expenditures, construction projects, and orders placed abroad, the estimate of expenditures for 1944 shows a decrease of approximately 7 per cent as compared with 1943. The rate of production in terms of dollar values reaches its peak in the first quarter of 1944.
In my last report, which was submitted to the house in June last, I pointed out that certain of our production targets had been attained. In the intervening months we have reached more of these objectives. I also stated in my last report that this did not necessarily mean any slackening of the overall effort. It did, of course, involve considerfMr. Howe.]
able programme revision, with some items reduced and others expanded. The house will understand that we must always allow for cancellations and changes in type when we attempt a long-range forecast of a production programme in time of war. It is possible to sketch the broad outlines of the programme, but there are bound to be variations, due to the changing character of the war, which cannot be anticipated. The changing strategy of war makes obsolete certain types of equipment, and creates the need for entirely new types of equipment. Generally speaking, the forecast of programme changes which I made last June has been realized in fact. I make this comment because I find a tendency on the part of some to express great alarm that in recent months there should have been changes in programme which have necessitated the transfer of employees to other places of employment. I wish to record that I told the house last June that certain changes in programme would occur. It can hardly be suggested now that they come as a complete surprise. Unfortunately, these changes are inevitable in a war production programme. For the most part, our -manufacturing capacity is sufficiently flexible to meet the constant need for programme revision. In many cases, when orders have been cancelled we have been able to convert the manufacturing capacity to other uses. But there will always be certain- capacity which is single-purpose, and is not suitable for other types of manufacture. Reductions or cancellations of programme in such single-purpose plants mean reductions in personnel. We cannot justify the employment of men and the use of materials in the production of equipment for which there is no longer any need. The Department of Munitions and Supply is working in close cooperation with national selective service in finding other useful employment for any personnel affected by lay-offs.
Before giving the house the details of each of the major programmes, I shall give the highlights of each programme, showing the accomplishment to date and the general trend of the programme in the next twelve months.
In 1943 we produced 4,133 aircraft, as against 3,811 in 1942, for a total production as at March 1 of 11,390 aircraft. The value of planes produced in 1943 was 50 per cent higher than in 1942, due to the predominance of larger types of more intricate design. The aircraft production programme will continue to expand with a transfer of effort from trainer aircraft to combat aircraft.
Armoured fighting vehicles produced last year number 15,500, as against 12,500 in 1942, for a total production to March 1 of 34,000

War Appropriation-Supplies
units. The production of self-propelled mounts, and of other armoured fighting vehicles, will continue at a high rate in 1944.
The production of mechanical transport dropped from 192,000 units in 1942 to 175,000 units in 1943, but we manufactured heavier and more costly equipment in 1943 than in 1942. The total production to March 1 is 593,000 units. This continues to be a major programme, and although we will produce fewer units in 1944 than in 1943, they will be of a heavier type.
The production of artillery gun barrels, carriages, and mountings, both army and navy, considered as separate units, totalled 45,000 in 1943, as compared with 31,000 in 1942, for a total production to date of 84,000 units. There will be a further cut in the production of army guns and a slight increase in the production of naval guns.
The output of machine guns, rifles and other small arms, jumped from 325,000 in 1942 to 580,000 in 1943, for a total production of
1,000,000 units. Production in 1944 will be slightly greater than in 1943, but this is weighted by the production of several new stores which can be produced at a higher rate.
In 1943 we produced 30 million rounds of gun ammunition, as against 28 million rounds in 1942. The total production since war began is 62 million rounds. Production in 1944 will carry on at approximately the same rate as in 1943.
The production of small arms ammunition increased from 1-2 billion rounds in 1942 to 1-5 billion rounds in 1943, for a total production to date of 3-3 billion rounds. This programme will be reduced somewhat during 1944.
Our total net production of chemicals and explosives in 1943 was 1 billion pounds, as against 860 million pounds in 1942, for a total production to March 1 of 2-3 billion pounds. This programme also will be reduced, and we have already had to close down one major explosives plant.
We produced 150 cargo vessels, or 1 million 478 thousand deadweight tons, in 1943, as against 81 cargo vessels, or 838 thousand deadweight tons, in 1942. The total production to March 1, is 249 vessels. There will be a slight reduction in the programme during 1944.
In 1943 we produced 100 naval vessels, as against 117 in 1942. However, the programme in 1943 was of a much more difficult and costly nature, so that a comparison by number is hardly accurate. The total production of escort vessels since war began is 336. There will be some revisions in this programme, with, reductions of certain types and the production of new types. Actual deliveries of escort vessels and other types of new naval craft will be higher in 1944 than in 1943.
Of a total of 4,300 orders placed for small craft, we have delivered 3,600. Deliveries on this programme will continue in 1944 at approximately the same level as in 1943.
The production of instruments and communication equipment in dollar cost was 180 million in 1943, as compared with 84 million dollars in 1942. The total value of production since the beginning of the war is 320 million dollars. This continues to be an expanding programme.
There was a slight decline in defence and other construction projects undertaken by the Department of Munitions and Supply in 1943, when the total amount spent was 194 million dollars, as against 219 million dollars in 1942. We have spent on construction since war began, including housing, 675 million dollars. There will be a sharp reduction in defence building during 1944.
Purchases of personal equipment, foodstuffs, fuel, hardware and miscellaneous stores, totalled at December 31, 1943, 2 billion 988 million dollars.
That is, since the war.

Yes, the total from the beginning of the war.
I will now review each of the majoi programmes.
Aircraft: Of the 11,390 planes produced since the beginning of the war, over 2,000 have been first-line service aircraft. The balance of the programme is made up of trainer types, and one service type which is no longer used in front-line combat. Plane production in March, April, and May, 1943, totalled 971 craft, or an average of 324 planes a month. Production for the three months ending February 29 last was 1,309 planes, or an average of 436 monthly. This shows an increase in units of production of one-third, but the actual increase in poundage production is 50 per cent. Since the beginning of the war we have produced some twenty different types of aircraft. Despite the fact that we have had many programme changes, the general curve of production has been upward each year. There have been ups and downs in the number of planes produced, but the trend has been upward both in number and in weight.

Will the
minister permit a question?
Yes.

Will he
make it clear how much, in percentage or otherwise, of this production is Canadian-made and how much is imported? I think that would be useful information.
War Appropriation-Supplies
Well, Mr. Chairman, the airframe is almost completely Canadian made, but we do not make engines.

I just
wanted to find out how much Canadian content there was.
Practically all the instruments are now made in Canada, and I think veiy little is imported except the engines.
Are the propellers made in Canada?
Yes.

Would the minister explain how the statement he is making connects with this schedule? For instance, he is referring to aircraft construction. I do not know what item of this that could be connected with.

I might point out that the function of the department is to do purchasing for the various branches of the government and the foreign governments, and they sflpply the money. We do not vote money for purchases of this kind. No. 7 would be the item it ties in with. But I assume that, in discussing the department, hon. members will want to know what the department is doing.

We expect to produce 4,312 aircraft in 1944, for a total poundage of 21,430,000. In the number of planes produced per month, we reached our peak last January, with a total output of 455 aircraft. The shift in programme from trainer to service types tends to reduce the output in terms of numbers, since one service type may involve fifty times the man-hours employed on the production of a primary trainer.
Including the overhaul plants, the primary contractors and the sub-contractors, there are now 122,000 persons employed in aircraft manufacture, of whom 39,000 are women. The overhaul of aircraft in operation, in Canada, has become a major industry. We are now overhauling some 200 planes and approximately 1,000 engines each month.
I shall now give the house some details of the individual programmes, dealing first with the trainer programme.

We are building three trainer craft, the Cornell, a primary trainer, the Harvard, a secondary trainer, and the Anson, a twin-engined trainer. We are also producing the Norseman, which was used formerly as a service craft, and is now used for military transport. Because the trainer programme is tied in closely with the British commonwealth air training plan, there has been a marked falling-off in requirements for trainer aircraft in recent months, and consequently we plan to produce in 1944 considerably fewer trainer planes than in 1943. Production of Cornells in 1943 was at the rate of 125 per month, for a total production to March 1 of 1,579. The rate of production in 1944 will be 50 per month. During 1943 Harvard production was scheduled at 100 per month. This rate of production will continue until the end of 1944. We have delivered to date 1,849 Harvards. The house will recall that the Arison, the most important item in the trainer programme, wras one of our most difficult production jobs in the early years of the war. Federal Aircraft Limited, a crown company, was set up to administer this programme. During 1943 deliveries were made at the rate of 70 per month, total deliveries to March 1 being 2,413 aircraft. Of that number 560 have been of a new type, which is equipped with moulded veneer fuselage and a more powerful engine. In keeping with the current needs of the air training plan, the Anson production schedule has been curtailed very sharply, and production during 1944 will be at the rate of 35 per month.
There is a tendency on the part of some of our critics to make light of the trainer programme. I would remind the house that we could not have maintained the output of aircrew which is needed for combat service overseas if we had not had a plentiful supply of trainer aircraft. One of the-main objectives of the aircraft production programme from its very inception was to supply all the trainer aircraft needed for the operation of the British commonwealth air training plan. I am glad to say that we have succeeded in that objective.
Our production of service aircraft is now confined to four world-famous types, each of which is unsurpassed in its class. These are the Lancaster, the Mosquito, the PBY Catalina and the Curtis dive bomber. I say at once that each of these programmes has taxed the skill and ingenuity of our aircraft industry. In each case very elaborate tooling was required, and one of the most difficult bottlenecks has been the need to absorb and train large numbers of personnel concurrently

War Appropriation-Supplies
with production. I make no excuse for the time required to reach production forecasts. Anyone who had had any association with the aircraft industry in this country, in the United States or in the United Kingdom knows that it is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to forecast with any degree of accuracy the time required to bring into full production a plane of complicated design which has not been produced in large numbers elsewhere. More problems have arisen in connection with the production of the Mosquito than of any other plane manufactured in Canada. We have maintained close touch with the manufacturer of this aircraft in the United Kingdom, and I may tell the house that the English producer has experienced the same difficulties that have been met here. In this connection, I think it may be of value to place on Hansard a table showing the comparative statistics on the production of the Mosquito in the De Havilland Plant in the United Kingdom and in the De Havilland Plant in Canada. In giving these figures I ask you to remember that the design originated with the English company.

In monthly production, we reached our highest figure in Pebruary, with an output of 33 planes. Total production to date is 183 planes. We hope to reach a production of 52 per month by June next.
The plant producing Mosquitos is now under direct government control, and I am satisfied that the management is doing everything possible to accelerate the rate of production.
Turning now to the Lancaster programme, this, as hon. members know, is the largest four-engined bomber of this war to date. Considering the fact that our aircraft industry is but five years old, I think we may take some satisfaction from the knowledge that we are now producing one of the finest types of heavy bomber aircraft in existence. Here again there have been exceptional^ technical difficulties arising from the complexity of the design and elaborate tooling and engineering. Up to March 20, we had delivered 39 Lancasters. Of the two planes delivered to Trans-Canada Air Lines, one has established
a transatlantic flying record. Regarding the quality of Lancasters produced in Canada, I should like to quote from a letter which I have received from Sir Stafford Cripps, the British minister of aircraft production. The excerpt reads as follows:
I have just heard how well the first production Canadian Lancaster fared at the arrival conference held last week. My experts tell me that this is the best first production aircraft out of all the north American ones that they have ever seen. Since we have dealt*with some 90 of them, this is indeed a high compliment, and I should like' to offer my warmest congratulations to everybody concerned on an outstanding piece of work.
Our largest monthly production was in February, with an output of 9 aircraft. We hope to reach a monthly output of 17 by May and 30 by December. Victory Aircraft Limited, a crown company, is in charge of the Lancaster programme.
The PBY Catalina flying boat is one of the largest and most intricate aircraft produced on this continent. To date, we have delivered 273 Catalinas, with peak production in December, 1943, when we turned out 37 planes. This programme will continue until the end of 1944, with monthly production rising to the rate of 50.
The Curtis dive bomber did not come into production as early as we had anticipated, because of a great many modifications of design in the early stages of the programme. The design of this plane has now been frozen. Current monthly production is at the rate of 20 per month, and we hope to reach a production rate of 70 per month by midsummer and 130 per month by December, 1944. There are two plants engaged on this programme, one of which came into production in September, 1943; the other in October of that year.
In closing my remarks on aircraft production, may I repeat what I have said in this house on previous occasions. When the war began, we had an aircraft industry with some 1,000 employees. The industry had produced only very simple types of aircraft and these in small numbers. We now have an industry which employs 122,000 people and which is producing combat aircraft of the. latest and finest types. I do not pretend that I am satisfied with current rates of production, but I do say that, considering our small beginnings and the magnitude and complexity of the programme we have undertaken, the performance to date is a creditable one.
Military vehicles.-Canada has established a very fine reputation for the quality of its mechanical transport. As the house is aware, a large part of the transport used by the 8th Army in the African campaign was manu-
War Appropriation-Supplies

faetured in Canada. When the enemy was driven out of Africa, a number of military documents were seized. Among them was found a German reconnaissance order, which when translated reads as follows:
For the reconnaissance, as indeed for every desert reconnaissance, only captured Canadian trucks are to be employed, since German trucks stick in the sand too often.
Military transport from Canadian plants is in demand in every combat zone. Because of this, volume of production will continue at the highest possible level. There will, however, be some reduction in the number of units produced, since the emphasis is shifting from the 2-wheel drive chassis to the 4-wheel drive chassis, which requires more man-hours per unit. The current rate of wheeled vehicle production is 13,000 monthly. In addition to the production of complete units, the automotive industry and component manufacturers are devoting a large part of their capacity to the production of spare parts. The maintenance of transport in the field is possible only with adequate supplies of parts. During 1943 our spare parts production averaged in cost 7jj million dollars per month. During 1944 we expect to reach a figure of 11| million dollars per month. The production of armoured cars and reconnaissance cars was discontinued in 1943. The production of scout cars also stopped for a brief time, but will begin again this quarter, following the introduction of new designs. We also expect to produce some hundreds of armoured trucks during 1944. The programme in 1944 will include the manufacture of workshop lorries at the rate of 200 per month. In 1943 we completed all our orders for tanks. The capacity which was created for the manufacture of tanks is being used to produce self-propelled gun mounts, tank turrets and railway equipment. Our production of self-propelled gun-mounts, which operate on tank chassis, amounted to 1,928 in 1943. The current rate of production of this equipment is 150 per month. We have large orders under way for locomotives and other railway equipment for the combat areas. Locomotives for shipment overseas are now being produced at the rate of 24 per month. Our railway equipment manufacturers are working to full capacity on the production of freight cars and other types of rolling stock for home and overseas use. The universal carrier will, continue to be produced in 1944 at a rate of 900 per month. To date, we have delivered 24,000 universal carriers.

Before the minister leaves that point, is there any reasonable expectation of some automotive power being released for civilian purposes in Canada?

He knows, as I do, that there is a tremendous demand now for that sort of thing for essential services.

We are producing a limited number of trucks, the fewest w.e think will meet essential 'demands. We are being pressed for the greatest possible output of military vehicles, there being a shortage on all fronts.
The minister recognizes there is a need.
Yes. We are maintaining that. As far as passenger cars are concerned I am afraid we cannot do anything.
I am not suggesting that.
We are, however, building trucks for civilian purposes.	'
Has there been any easing on purely military transport?

No.
Communications.-It is difficult to speak of the communications and signals programme without burdening the house with excessive details. However, I shall give some round figures on the value of our production and a few highlights of the programme. The value of our production in communications in 1940 was one million dollars, in 1942 60 million dollars; and in 1943 136 million dollars. The radio and communications industry is now operating at a level some eighteen times greater than in 1939. We have orders on our books to the value of 400 million dollars, and we do not expect to reach peak production until the second quarter of 1944. To illustrate the diversity of the programme, I might point out that there are approximately 4,500 different items in current production by some fifty prime contractors and several hundred subcontractors. The items include: Amplifiers, antennce, cable, radio compasses, remote control units, radio direction finders, signalling lamps, power generators, quartz crystals, 25 types of radio receivers, 23 types of radio transmitters, 19 types of transmitting and receiving sets, 6 types of telephones, radio tubes, and switchboards, to mention but a few.
Some twenty major types of radar equipment have been developed for a variety of applications, ranging from one type for antiaircraft defence having 60,000 components, and 270 radio tubes, mounted in several large trucks, to small compact airborne units used for submarine detection at sea and target location on land.
Obviously, this is a type of equipment in which there must be constant and rapid

War Appropriation-Supplies
improvement if we are to maintain our superiority over the enemy. This means frequent change in design, which in turn requires great flexibility in production methods. A major factor in the production of communications equipment has been the contribution of Research Enterprises Limited, a crown company which was set up in the early months of the war. In 1943 the total value of the communications equipment produced by the company was 60 million dollars. The company also has produced optical equipment and instruments to the value of 10 million dollars. From its optical glass, Research manufactures binoculars, range finders, and a wide variety of other instruments.
In addition to these programmes, the communication industry is also producing fire control boxes and other sonic devices of many types, including torpedo components and a wide variety of gun-laying instruments. The entire communication programme is coordinated by the signals production branch of the Department of Munitions and Supply. This has resulted in the elimination of waste through the simplification of manufacturing practices and the more efficient use of manufacturing capacity.
Defence Communications Limited.-In addition to the production of communication equipment, the department is also building an extensive communication system for the armed services, through the agency of Defence Communications Limited, a crown company.
This company was set up early in 1943, to coordinate existing communication services, and to establish new services in eastern Canada. The communication system utilizes existing wire, telegraph and wireless facilities of the three armed services and of commercial operators. These services have been supplemented by the building of new facilities to the value of some three million dollars.
Guns. There have been drastic reductions in the production of army guns during 1943, as forecast in my statement of June last. The downward trend in gun production has been offset to a degree by the programming of certain new types of guns and new mountings. There will be further downward revisions during 1944. I am asked frequently why plant capacity which was created to manufacture army guns should not now be in full use. The reason is that we now have supplied the current and prospective needs of the armed services. Where it is possible, we are converting this plant capacity to other uses, but in many cases we think it necessary to maintain plants and equipment in working condition for stand-by purposes.
The current army gun production programme includes five types of barrels and several types of mountings, together with detector and fuse setting equipment required for the 3-7 inch anti-aircraft gun. Some of the manufacturing capacity which otherwise would have been idle is working on orders for China. We are now shipping to China two types of antiaircraft guns, as well as 6-pounder guns.
While the need for army guns is declining, we are continuing in full production of naval guns and mountings. This programme includes three types of naval gun barrels and eight types of mountings. We will come into production of another type of gun and mounting in the immediate future. Among the various companies engaged in naval gun production is National Railways Munitions Limited, a crown company, which has been a most efficient contractor.
Small Arms. In the small arms field, we discontinued, in 1943, the production of four types, the Boys antLtank rifle, two types of machine guns and the 3-inch mortar. We have just come into production with the 9mm. pistol, the 20mm. universal mounting, and the Polsten 20mm. automatic gun, a most modern and effective weapon. We have also begun producing a modified version of the Bren gun. Total production of Bren guns to date is
155,000.	Rifle production from the plant of Small Arms Limited, a crown company, was at a rate of 35,000 per month in 1943, for a total production of 530,000 to the end of 1943.
All weapons?
Five hundred and thirty thousand, all rifles.

That does not include
Stens?

No. The current rate of production is 25,000 per month. The reduction is due to lower requirements of this store. Sten gun production by Small Arms Limited, which reached a peak of 8,500 per month in 1943, will continue in production at 5,000 a month during 1944. Here again the' reduced output is due to smaller requirements. There will be some increase in the production of 2-inch mortars, which will increase from 400 a month in 1943 to 600 a month during 1944. The production of bomb throwers will continue at a rate of 3,000 per month. In general, there will not be any great shrinkage in the small arms programme during the first half of 1944, but there may be considerable curtailment in the programme during the latter part of the year, when many contracts run out. Nevertheless, the small arms orders now on hand will mean a production in 1944 slightly in excess of that of 1943.

Ammunition. The output of gun ammunition during 1943 was 30 million rounds. In addition to this, there was produced a total of 40 million cartridge cases and many millions of fuses and other components. A substantial proportion of these components are filled in Canadian shell-filling plants before being shipped abroad. In 1944 we shall fill some 33 types, including bombs and grenades. Among them is the projectile for the new Piat, an anti-tank weapon; an- anti-aircraft shell; two new grenades, and anti-submarine ammunition. There are in all more than 130 plants now engaged in manufacturing gun ammunition and components. In all, the programme involves the production of 154 varieties of shell, or other ammunition components. This programme will be curtailed1 somewhat, with operation during the balance of 1944 at approximately 75 per cent of peak capacity. Curtailment in the ammunition programme will also result in a decline in the output of fuses, primers, gaines, and cartridge cases.
Small Arms Ammunition. During the last half of 1943, production of small arms ammunition totalled 775 million rounds, ranging in calibre from '22 inch to 1 inch. This output included more than thirty different types. The major part of the production is carried on in two government arsenals. In the summer of 1943 the programmes were revised, with a shift to heavy calibre types. The current production rate is 118 million rounds per month. The new programme is scheduled to reach a rate of 122 million rounds per month.
Chemicals and Explosives. We reached peak production on chemicals and explosives during 1943. Curtailments in the ammunition programme will require about a 20 per cent reduction in the output of explosives. The only explosive for which the demand has increased is RDX. In line with declining requirements, rifle cordite production has been discontinued at two plants. TNT production and other explosives produced in the plant at Nobel, Ontario, have also been discontinued. The demand for chemicals such as ammonium nitrate, hexachlorethane, and some other chemicals, will continue at about the same level in 1944 as in 1943. The chemicals and explosives programme is tied in very closely with the shell-filling programme . The whole operation, which is administered by Allied War Supplies Corporation, a crown company, involves approximately fifty chemical, explosive, and shell-filling projects.
I would like to say a word here about the contribution of Canadian science in the development of chemicals and explosives. Canadian chemists have discovered the most effective method of manufacturing RDX, the
TMr. Howe.]
new super-explosive. They have devised improved and important changes in the manufacture of TNT. Canadian scientists have developed a process for large-scale manufacture of fuse powders. Hitherto, this had been considered more of a craft than a manufacturing process.
Shipbuilding.-Our shipbuilding programme from its inception was divided into two parts, the naval vessel programme, under the direction of the naval shipbuilding branch of the department, and the cargo vessel programme, which has been administered by Wartime Merchant Shipping Limited, a crown company. We have also had two crown companies actually engaged in the production of naval ships, the Toronto Shipbuilding Company, which operates a yard and fitting out berth, and Quebec Shipyards Limited, operating two shipyards and a fitting out berth. In December last it was decided to consolidate the naval and cargo vessel programmes. The whole programme is now under the general direction of the director general of shipbuilding of the Department of Munitions and Supply. Wartime Merchant Shipping Limited, which now becomes Wartime Shipbuilding Limited, will assume responsibility for the supervision of the larger naval vessel programme as well as the cargo vessel programme. The small boat programme, including wooden minesweepers, tugs and other miscellaneous craft, will continue to be under the immediate direction of the shipbuilding branch. This consolidation will eliminate certain duplication in servicing, and will make for more efficient operation. Late in 1943, a change in management was made in the Toronto Shipbuilding Company, with very satisfactory results. As a part of the recent change in the administration of the programme, the Toronto Shipbuilding Company has surrendered its charter and will now operate as a crown plant under the supervision of Wartime Shipbuilding Limited1.
I should like now to give some details of the two programmes, dealing first with naval vessels.
Naval Shipbuilding.-To the end of February we had delivered 336 escort and patrol vessels, including 28 frigates, 104 single screw corvettes, 92 steel minesweepers, 34 wooden minesweepers, and 78 Fairmile patrol boats. In addition to these deliveries, we launched 75 vessels of these types which are now being fitted out.
Under the naval vessel programme, we have also delivered three types of landing craft, the 52-foot ramped cargo lighter, the 72-foot Minca barge, and the 51-foot landing vessel. Total deliveries of this type of vessel at the

War Appropriation-Supplies
end of February amounted to 925. In 1943 our naval yards produced 45 tugs and two auxiliary tankers.
In addition to these major items in the programme, we have had orders for some 4,300 small craft. Of these, 3,600 have been delivered. The naval yards have also constructed a wide variety of special purpose vessels, including base and supply ships, concrete and wooden gate vessels, a floating dry dock, railway barges, steel and wooden derrick scows, ammunition and stores lighters, transport and salvage barges, tenders, target towing vessels, and 24 motor torpedo boats.
Late in 1943 we were advised of reduced requirements for certain types of escort vessels. The scheduled deliveries for 1944 will be 44 frigates, 18 single screw corvettes, 29 steel minesweepers, 45 wooden minesweepers, and 11 Fairmiles. This programme, although it is considerably less in volume than we had originally planned, will still represent in dollar cost our highest actual delivery of escort vessels. Deliveries of landing craft, small craft, and miscellaneous vessels, will be at a slightly higher level in 1944 than in 1943.
Some of the shipbuilding capacity which has been released through reductions in orders for escort vessels will be taken up with orders for a new type of landing vessel. We have also placed contracts for six 3,600-ton oil tankers in two of our naval yards. At the present time, ten of our shipyards and three outfitting yards are engaged on the naval programme. Five small yards are building other steel vessels such as tugs, lighters and auxiliary oil tankers and 62 smaller yards are engaged on the small boat programme.
In addition to the plants actually engaged in ship construction, there are the many plants turning out ship fittings and components.
Employment in the yards and in allied industries working on the naval shipbuilding programme is now running at 50,000 persons.
Cargo vessels: Our deliveries of cargo vessels at the end of February of this year amounted to two hundred and thirty-four 10,000-ton vessels and fifteen 4,700-tonners, making in all a delivery of 2,600,000 tons of shipping. We have planned for the delivery in 1944 of one hundred and two 10,000-ton vessels, including six which will be of a special type, and eighteen 4,700-ton vessels. At the present time, seven of our shipyards are engaged on the 10,000-ton programme and three of the smaller yards are producing 4,700-ton ships.
A word about the types of vessels we build:
First there is the North Sands, the original design for which came from England. We have made several modifications in this vessel,
increasing its deadweight tonnage from 9,300 to 10,350, and generally adapting it to Canadian construction methods.
Then there is the Victory Ship, which differs from the coal-burning North Sands type in that it is an'oil burner, with water tube boilers instead of Scotch marine boilers. It has more elaborate fittings and better living accommodation for the crew.
The third class, the Canadian type, uses the same basic hull as the North Sands and Victory types but can burn either coal or oil. This type was designed in Canada to provide an efficient general cargo ship for Canadian operations.
We are also building the Victory Tanker, which is a Victory freighter converted into an oil-carrying vessel.
Of the 10,000-ton ships scheduled for delivery in 1944, the majority are of the Victory type, but all of the 10,000-ton cargo vessel orders placed in recent months are for ships of the Canadian type.
The 4,700-ton vessels are all of the William Gray class. I might point out that these are by no means small ships. They are 328 feet long, carry a substantial payload, and are ideal for coastal trading. We have orders on hand for this ship which will carry over well into 1945. I would point out to the house that it is not the policy to freeze ship designs. Many modifications in design have been made, and a special technical committee is now studying this question with a view to improving the operating economy of cargo vessels.
In addition to the construction of cargo vessels, certain of our west coast yards are engaged on alterations to aircraft carriers for the British Admiralty.
Of our total production Of cargo vessels to March 1, fifty-four 10,000-tonners, including 10 tankers and thirteen 4,700-tonners, are in Canadian service. These vessels have been delivered to Park Steamship Company, Limited, the crown company which arranges for and supervises the operation of cargo vessels under Canadian registry. The balance of the output has gone to the maritime commission of the United States, the British Ministry of War Transport, and one 4700-ton vessel recently was turned over to the Government of Australia under the mutual aid agreement. It is anticipated that thirty 10,000-ton vessels, including 3 tankers, will be added to the Canadian merchant fleet by the end of August.
As the house is aware, vessels for Canadian service are requisitioned by the Canadian shipping board, which has first call on our output of cargo vessels. The route over which
War Appropriation-Supplies

the ships will operate is also determined by the Canadian shipping board. The selection of the operating company is made by Park Steamship Company, which signs the operating agreement on behalf of the government, and maintains close supervision' over operating costs. The operating agreements are basically the same as used by the British Ministry of War Transport with the various British shipping companies. The operating fees are modest, and all profits after the payment of fees accrue to the Park Steamship Company. I may say that operating results to date have been most satisfactory.
Ship repairs and salvage: As I have reported to the house in previous years, a large part of our shipbuilding capacity has been devoted exclusively to ship repairs. We have had to expend 10 million dollars in the expansion of ship repair facilities. Since the Royal Canadian Navy assumed complete responsibility for the north Atlantic convoy, the burden on our ship repair facilities has increased tremendously. In addition to the repairing and outfitting of naval vessels, the major part of the servicing of the merchant fleet has been .done on this side of the Atlantic. Bare figures hardly give a real picture of the magnitude of this undertaking. However, since January 1940 to December 1943 there have been repaired in Canada 25,000 vessels, naval and merchant. Five thousand of these were dry-docked for major overhaul.
Salvage operations have been carried on in conjunction with the control of ship repairs, resulting in the recovery of many valuable cargoes.
The destroyer programme is also under the direction of the controller of ship repairs and salvage. The boilers have been installed in our first destroyer, and the turbine units will be installed this summer. A second destroyer will be launched early this spring; the keel of a third destroyer has been laid and a fourth will be laid shortly. This programme has challenged the best that Canada can offer in the way of technical skill. I am glad to say that our Canadian engineering firms and workmen are measuring up to the test.
Construction.-Since the beginning of the war, the Department of Munitions and Supply has awarded construction contracts totalling some 455 million dollars. Practically all of this outlay has been for the construction of facilities for the armed services, such as air training schools, operational airports, naval establishments and army barracks. Up to 1943, the cost of construction projects averaged 100 million dollars per year. There will be a
TMr. Howe.]
sharp reduction during 1944, when we expect to spend 40 million dollars on construction projects. This programme has been in part under the direction of the director general of construction of the Department of Munitions and Supply and in part under the civil aviation division of the Department of Transport, which reports to the Minister of Munitions and Supply.
Housing.-Early in the war, it became apparent that emergency housing would have to be provided in areas where there was a heavy concentration of new war industry, or where new munitions plants were being established in locations remote from centres of population. This war emergency housing programme has been in charge of Wartime Housing Limited, a crown company. To date, the company has constructed 17,700 houses, 13 hostels, 69 staff houses, 15 bunk houses, 19 dining halls, 30 schools and 22 community buildings. Occupancy is currently about 98 per cent. Each housing unit is in charge of an administrator, who is responsible for the collection of rents and for other matters incidental to the operation of the unit. In 1943, tb? gross revenue of Wartime Housing Limited from rentals was slightly in excess of 6 million dollars. As those of you who have visited these housing units know, we have tried to make each of them a self-contained community unit, with all the services that a modern community requires. I think we have been particularly fortunate in our tenant relations. Under the guidance of Wartime Housing Limited, more than 80 social and educational programmes are in progress in these communities. These include child care and baby centres, supervised recreation for children and adolescents, nutrition courses, libraries, handicrafts, home improvement and garden clubs, and group health schemes. The objective always has been to minimize the dislocation in family and community life which is a by-product of war.1
Now that our production programme has reached its peak, the need for the provision of emergency housing has passed. The responsibility of Wartime Housing Limited will now be to administer and maintain its properties. In this connection, I would remind the house that Wartime Housing Limited was established for a specific purpose-to provide housing where and when a shortage of accommodation was likely to interfere with a munitions programme. The company has no jurisdiction in the field of general housing, which has continued to be the responsibility of the national housing administration.

General Purchases. The general purchasing division of the Department of Munitions and Supply is responsible for the procurement of personal equipment and the many items of service stores, such as food, fuel, medical supplies, hardware, etc. Total purchases to the end of 1943 amount to 2 billion 988 million dollars. We anticipate some reduction in the volume of purchases of this kind, but so long as the war lasts, and we continue to have hundreds of thousands of men and women under arms, the purchase of clothing, foodstuffs and medical supplies will continue to be a major factor in our budget. For example, we are now working on orders for 800,000 complete battle dress suits and 560,000 'pairs of boots. Speaking of medical supplies, on the requisition of the Department of National Defence we have created recently facilities for the production of penicillin. We expect to obtain this very important medical store in volume supply at an early date.
Early in 1943, a crown company, known as North West Purchasing Limited, was set up to purchase requirements of the Canadian armed forces and the United States armed forces in northwestern Canada. During the height of construction activities in that area, the expenditures of North West Purchasing Limited were running at the rate of 1 million dollars per month. With the completion of certain of the larger construction projects, we anticipate a considerable falling off in the volume of purchases.
The Plateau Company, a crown company established in 1940 to purchase and stockpile raw silk, was abolished in 1943. The functions of this company, which also include the handling of limited quantities of raw cotton, kapok and nylon, have been absorbed by Melbourne Merchandising Limited, another crown company which has been responsible for the purchase of bulk wool required by the government for war purposes, and for the allocation of yarn for certain types of production.
The house will remember that under the terms of the Hyde Park agreement, Canada and the United States agreed to exchange materials and equipment required in their respective war programmes. War Supplies Limited, the crown company which was set up in 1941 to act as the agency in placing orders in Canada for delivery to the United States, has had a busy year.
Controls. I have been speaking of the various production programmes under the direction of the Department of Munitions and Supply. Each of these programmes is dependent on- adequate supplies of raw and primary materials. This brings me to the second
phase of the department's activities, the work of the wartime industries control board. The board consists of seventeen controllers and a chairman, who is responsible for coordinating their activities. I shall preface my remarks on the individual controls by pointing out, as I have done before, that we have established controls only where conservation of a particular material was indispensable to the success of the production programme.
That is almost everywhere.

No; only seventeen. By the same token, we relax controls whenever there is an easing of the supply position. This may be due in some cases to the building up of stocks of materials to the point where current and anticipated requirements have been satisfied, or it may be due to the falling off of a demand for a particular material due to changes in the requirements of the war services.
Coal. In normal times, we consume annually in this country approximately 26 million tons of coal, of which 14 million tons are produced in Canada and the balance imported from the United States. By 1943, our consumption had increased to 46 million tons, of which over 28 million tons have been imported. These figures will give the house some idea of our coal problem. Despite some improvement in the over-all production picture, there is no doubt that we shall have a serious coal problem on our hands for the duration of the war. As the house is aware, the problem of coal supply, like many other Canadian problems, differs from area to area. The output of domestic coals and lignites in western Canada has increased sufficiently to provide for home needs and to permit some export to the United States. In the maritimes, labour shortages and transportation problems have created shortages. We must have increased production if this area is to be self-contained. Central Canada is dependent to a large extent on coal imported from the United States. Our arrangements with the United States for the supply of bituminous and anthracite have been most satisfactory. While supplies of bituminous coal have been ample, we have not been able to obtain sufficient anthracite to meet our demands. Because of this, we have had to ask the householder in central Canada to use a certain proportion of bituminous coal. Some increase in the production of coke has helped to ease the situation.
Various measures have been adopted in an endeavour to stimulate Canadian production. The emergency coal production board, which operates under the coal controller, has provided financial assistance to mine operators in
War Appropriation-Supplies

various forms, especially in cases where the operation normally would be uneconomic. The board has also financed extensive stripping operations in western Canada. Late last summer, a fuel conservation programme was inaugurated for the industrial and commercial user and the householder; this has resulted in great savings in annual consumption. There was a time, early in the fall, when it seemed unlikely that we could fill our coal requirements. At that time, certain steps were taken by the coal controller to prevent hardship during the winter months. Regional offices were set up across Canada, with regional administrators to supervise the distribution of coal in the region. I am glad to say that some increase in production, the effects of the conservation programme, plus the great blessing of a mild winter, have dissipated our fears. However, we must not forget that we cannot count on an equally mild winter in the heating season of 1944-45.
Another winter coming!

The coal which is mined today, and in the next few months, will be marketed for next winter's supply. If we are to meet all of our requirements, industrial and domestic, we must continue a policy of strict conservation, and we must raise the level of production in those areas where production is now falling behind the demand,
Wood Fuel: Our annual consumption of wood fuel is 10 million cords, and about 90 per cent of this is produced by the farmer. The farmer also accounts for the consumption of about 60 per cent of our wood fuel cut. The balance of the cut is marketed in our cities and towns. Because of the severity of the winter 1942-43, stocks in hand fell off to an alarming degree. Wood Fuel Control was established to stimulate production, and to supervise the distribution of wood, in order that there might be no hardship during the present winter. The policy of subsidies, which was initiated last spring and extended through the winter months, did much to improve production. In addition to the production subsidy, transportation subsidies have also been paid, in order to facilitate the movement of wood to probable distressed areas. The wood fuel controller also initiated a number of special cutting projects, as a means of building up Government-owned banks of wood fuel, which could be held in reserve and shipped to any areas where distress was imminent. Studies of the consumption of wood fuel made it possible to determine the areas of high consumption. In these areas a special effort was

made to have the cities and smaller municipalities undertake their own wood cutting, wood storing and wood distribution programmes. I am glad to report that most of the municipalities responded in splendid fashion to this proposal. These various measures, coupled with the extremely mild winter, have enabled us to meet all wood fuel requirements. We are hopeful that the fine weather we have had this winter will bring about a return to normal production on the farms. However, to ensure the building up of adequate stocks for the next heating season, the policy of paying production and transportation subsidies will continue in effect until June 1st. At that time we will review the policy in the light of the then existing supply of fuel wood.

Power. Due to the expansion of our Canadian power resources and the various conservation measures which have been initiated by the power controller, Canada passed through the peak of all power demands at the turn of the year without serious shortage or inconvenience. However, the situation is still extremely tight, and we can look for no immediate relaxation of the various control orders which have been brought into effect to conserve power. Shortages of gas have occurred in western Ontario, but the new gas plant in Hamilton is now in complete operation, and it is hoped that the essential needs of this area can be met.
Machine Tools. This was one of our most important controls in the early stages of the production programme. The control still has a vital part to play in the production programme, but the nature of its work has changed considerably. Oil. I have recently made a statement with regard to gasoline and oil products. Our position continues to be serious. Improvement in the transportation of crude has been more than offset by the ever-increasing demands for gasoline and oil products in the combat areas. As the tempo of the offensive mounts, the demand for aviation gasoline and other oil products also increases. This means that we cannot hope for any relaxation in the present conservation programme. As already announced, the rationing plan for the motorist will continue without important change. While we are unable to obtain as large quantities of the light grades of crude as formerly, we have been able to increase our imports of the heavy grades. Because of this, we have a surplus of heavy fuel oils and asphalt. This will permit considerable relaxation in the use of heavy fuel oils, and asphalt is now on the free list. It should be noted thsit light fuel oil, used for domestic heating, is in the same position as gasoline, in very short supply.
There was some misunderstanding after the statement I made a month ago. Many householders thought I was indicating a better situation for light fuel oil. That is not the case. Light fuel oil, of course, is in the same class as gasoline, because it can be made into gasoline by a different process of refining; so that we must have the same conservation programme in the homes for fuel oil as we have in the motor cars for gasoline.
Is the difference in specific gravity?
Yes.
It is purely a matter of specific gravity of the oil?

Pretty well, yes.
During the past year, a new Canadian refinery, and a new alkylate plant, came into production. This new production will increase substantially the supply of aviation gasoline for the use of the British Commonwealth Air Training plan. Nevertheless, we are still in very short supply of aviation gasoline.

Of these, six have been completed and are now producing oil. We expect the balance of the wells to be in production by the end of June.
I had hoped to be able to give final reports on the results of the investigation of the production of oil from bituminous sands in northern Alberta. This work is being carried out under the direction of the Department of Mines and Resources. There is no technical

Rubber.-I have explained to the house in previous reports that Canada has had to depend for her supplies of raw rubber on quotas which are allocated from the united nations' stock pile. This stock pile has been a dwindling asset, and our problem has been to bring in production of synthetic rubber in time to avoid a shortage, which would have crippled our production programme. We have reached the point where I am able to say that we have won the race. The government-owned plant at Sarnia, which is administered by the Polymer Corporation, a crown company, is now in production. The estimated annual output of the plant, operating at full capacity, will be 34,000 long tons of buna-S and 4,000 long tons of butyl. The plant is a self-contained unit, producing butyl rubber, and styrene and butadiene, which are combined to produce buna-S rubber. The styrene plant came into production last July, the butadiene plant in February of this year. The production of buna-S rubber began at half capacity last September, with the use of styrene produced at the plant, and butadiene imported from the United States. Now that the butadiene unit is in production, imports from the United States will terminate. Production of buna-S is currently at the rate of 2500 tons per month, and butyl rubber at 150 tons per month. Production of buna-S should reach full capacity by May, and production of butyl by July. It is worth noting that the Polymer plant has no counterpart anywhere. Some plants produce one or more ingredients of synthetic, others produce finished synthetic. The Polymer plant produces all of the ingredients of synthetic rubber and manufactures two finished synthetics.
The production of synthetic rubber on this continent in commercial quantities is a new venture. The process which has been used by Polymer is similar to that adopted in the synthetic rubber programme in the United States. I may tell the house that Polymer has come into production in as short a space of time as any of the synthetic rubber projects with which it can be compared. With the Polymer plant in full production, we will be able to meet war and strictly essential requirements. We will not be able to give any great relief to the ordinary civilian user. It is
expected that 900,000 tires will be manufactured from synthetic rubber in 1944. A large part of these will go on military vehicles. The balance will be distributed to the public in accordance with the regulations of the tire rationing plan.
. A word about the quality of these tires. It is not possible yet to say that a synthetic tire matches the quality of a raw rubber tire. This department is conducting very extensive tests of synthetic tires, in conjunction with the United States army. The data obtained from these tests will, we hope, help to improve the quality of synthetic tires. So far as we can now estimate, the synthetic tire is about 80 per cent as efficient as a raw rubber tire. It is still necessary to use a certain proportion of natural rubber in the fabrication of tires for heavy duty and high speed operation.
We are now in a very easy position on rubber scrap. There are very large stock piles in Canada and in the United States.
The Fairmont Company, a crown company, continues to be the government agency for the purchase, sale and stock-piling of natural and synthetic rubber. The company works in close conjunction with the rubber controller and with the Polymer Corporation.

Supplies Control. The supplies of cork are now adequate, and restrictions respecting its use have been lifted except for the manufacture of linoleum, where shortage of other materials is the real limiting factor. While increased supplies of kapok have been forthcoming from India, our existing stocks must still be held exclusively for use in life-saving equipment of all types.
While the demand from Canadian war industry for nylon has declined, the restrictions on this fibre are still in effect, as our output is required overseas.
We have adequate supplies of the hard fibre for the manufacture of rope, but demands for the fishing industry are in excess of present productive capacity. Although the supply situation has improved somewhat, the demands from our ever-growing navy, and our fishermen, do not indicate any immediate relaxation of the controls affecting manila, sisal and henequen fibres.

War Appropriation-Supplies
As recently announced!, this control has been transferred to the Wartime Prices and Trade Board, since the problems with which it is concerned now have to do with civilian supply.
Steel. Our production of steel for 1943, amounting to 2 million 52S thousand tons, approximately doubled our production in 1939. Our total consumption in 1943 was 3 million 620 thousand tons, which means that we had to import from the United States, roughly, 1 million 92 thousand tons, or one-third of our requirements. During most of 1943, the steel position continued to be tight. We were able to meet war and essential needs only by the strictest conservation. The situation has changed very materially in recent months. Changes in the production programme, with the shift to lighter items, and the completion of the industrial expansion incidental to the war programme have been the principal factors. Therefore, it has been possible to lift some of the steel, restrictions, and seven of the control orders which were in effect in 1941, 1942 and 1943 have been lifted. Certain types of steel continue to be in short supply, mainly plates, sheets and strips. These will be subject to control until such time as the supply position improves. Sheets are extremely tight, both in Canada and in the United States, and I am unable to offer any hope that an increased supply will be available for the manufacture of roofing.
Motor Vehicle Control. This control was established to distribute the very small supply of trucks and' passenger automobiles which are available for civilian use, and to maintain the necessary flow of parts for the servicing of trucks andi passenger automobiles. We have not manufactured any passenger automobiles in Canada since April 1942. At that time, a number of passenger automobiles were placed in a government bank. These are allowed to be sold only under the regulations of the Motor Vehicle Controller, and in cases of the higest essentiality. So long as the demand for military vehicles and parts continues at its present level, there is no prospect of our being able to manufacture passenger automobiles.
Studies recently compiled for allied nations show a severe world shortage of trucks for military and civil needs during 1944. Because it is necessary that we maintain essential trucking services, we have manufactured each year a small quota of trucks. While we hope to increase the number that will be manufactured in 1944, we cannot begin to, make available sufficient trucks to meet the normal

demands. For this reason, a strict control of distribution must be maintained. We are dependent on the United States for our supply of heavy-duty trucks, an agreed quota of imports being fixed in co-operation with the War Production Board of the United States. Here again the number that can be obtained is considerably below the demand.
Will the minister say what the quota will be, or did he give the number?

Does the hon. member mean the total of domestic trucks? I shall be glad to give the figures later.
Chemicals.-Changes in war programmes have permitted some relaxation of controls in this field. Glycerine, formerly in very short supply, is now available for certain commercial uses. We are also now able to release coal tar for civilian purposes.

I
understood that glycerine was released for anti-freeze purposes, but from what I can make out among the garage men it was released for only a day or so and taken off the market again.

I shall be glad to look that up. Possibly another shortage developed and it was taken off. I know the control was taken off for a time.
Canada is an important source of supply of sulphuric acid and ethyl alcohol, for the United States. Our distilling capacity is now devoted entirely to the production of ethyl alcohol. Approximately one-half of our production is consumed in Canada. The balance is exported to the United States. Soda ash, a most important war chemical, is in very short supply, and we are dependent on importations from the United Kingdom and from the United States. In this control, as in others, supplies for civilian use will be released as circumstances permit.
Construction. The purpose of Construction Control is to conserve strategic materials, such as steel, lumber and other builders' supplies, by restricting non-essential building projects. In the early years of the war, the demands of military construction projects and of war industry for steel, lumber and other builders' supplies was very great. That demand has fallen off to a considerable extent, and is reflected in the easing of Construction Control regulations, particularly as they affect the construction of private dwelling houses. There has been some increase in the amount of money that can be expended on new building or repairs without a permit from the Controller of

War Appropriation-Supplies
Construction. The issuance of licences is still dependent to some extent on the labour situation in the area in which the building is located. The supply position has not yet improved sufficiently to permit the issuance of permits for public buildings, churches, places of amusement, etc., unless the circumstances are very exceptional. It is estimated that as of the 1st of February, 1944, there is a backlog of construction projects of 300 million dollars.
Transit control. Our urban transit facilities continue to carry a very heavy burden. So far as we can estimate, transit systems are now carrying twice as many passengers as in 1938. I do not think it is any exaggeration to say that many of these systems would have bogged down had we not established transit control.
Staggered hours arrangements have provided considerable relief. Under the Wartime Industrial Transit Plan, 54,000 private automobiles are now mobilized to transport war workers to and from their vtork. In addition to these measures, which were designed to relieve overburdening of transit facilities, we have made further curtailments of certain interurban bus services. Bus equipment is in very short supply, and these curtailments have enabled us to transfer buses to more essential routes. This control is tied in closely with rubber and gasoline conservation plans. The object of the rigid control of taxicabs, which is now being maintained, is to assist in the conservation of these very vital supplies. There has been a considerable reduction in the number of taxicabs in service without, I think, any undue inconvenience to, the public.
Priorities. Our priorities system continues to operate most satisfactorily. As the priorities office works in intimate association with the various production divisions, we have not found it necessary to institute a formal priorities procedure for deliveries of equipment and components produced in Canada. We thus have been able to arrange deliveries without recourse to an elaborate procedure, with its inevitable confusion and delay.
As we are dependent on the United States for much of our equipment, and many of our components, the Priorities Office has had to maintain a close working arrangement with the priorities division of the War Production Board of the United States. In the case of importations of equipment and components from the United States, we have conformed to the priority procedure laid down by the priorities division of the War Production Board. This will explain why a manufacturer, jobber or dealer who is importing equipment or
components from the United States must submit certain application forms to the Canadian priorities office. These applications are screened in the Canadian priorities office, but the final decision on the priority rests with the Priorities Division of the War Production Board.
Similarly, with importations from the United Kingdom, we have worked out an arrangement with the British Board of Trade whereby imports are kept at the minimum dictated by necessity. This has helped to conserve vital shipping space.
Before leaving the subject of controllers, I would point out that the duty of each controller has been to organize his industry for maximum production and to arrange distribution of his product in such a way that essential war needs can be met in full and the surplus distributed fairly among civilian users. Throughout a period of world scarcity of products essential to war production, Canadian production has never been seriously delayed for lack of raw materials. Under the direction of our controllers, our basic industries have been expanded greatly, always in time to meet the anticipated demand. Even materials which must be imported into Canada have been kept in supply. To me, the distribution of materials brought about by our controllers has been a miracle; certainly our record in that respect has not been equalled in any allied country. Now that the supply situation is easing, I am glad to pay this tribute to the work of our controllers, throughout a period of acute world scarcity.
War production in Canada has reached its peak, but the work of my Department has not lessened on that account. The termination of contracts, as dictated by the strategy of the war, is no easy task. Machinery for termination has been provided, which will, I believe, permit prompt conversion by the manufacturer of peacetime production, while fully protecting the government's interest in the cancelled contract.
There is also the problem of disposing of surplus materials, and surplus and obsolete equipment, purchased by the government for war purposes. A crown company, War Assets Corporation Limited, has been formed to deal with this problem, and parliament will be asked to consider legislation bearing on this problem.
Canada's great volume of war production has been made possible by full-out cooperation with the government, on the part of private industry, the producer, and the worker. My Department has called on each for a great effort, directed toward the winning of the war, and each has responded in full measure.
