This war is responsible for the destruction of life and property on an unprecedented scale, but we in Canada will receive some compensation through enlargements of our productive capacity which can later be directed into peacetime production. Reconversion of industry must wait until the demands of war are satisfied, but active steps are being taken to prepare for rapid reconversion when the time comes. Whether that time will be near, or distant, must depend on the progress of the war, but until the time comes, there must be neither slackening off in war production, nor diversion of producti-ve capacity away from war requirements. Let us concentrate on winning the war, while looking forward with confidence in our ability to meet the problems of conversion, when our paramount job is behind us.	.

The committee will understand that of necessity my observations will be of a general character, inasmuch as we have not the information that the minister was to give us, and shall not have it until such time as it is produced.
In the 'criticism I have to offer I shall try to be as constructive as possible. I am not anxious to get the minister into one of those moods into which he slips so easily and so often. My first criticism is in regard to the presentation of the estimates on February 11. Why can the department not furnish us with a break-down as other departments have done? If the advance information would be of comfort to the enemy, then I could understand it; but I cannot see why on that account the minister should be restrained from producing a proper break-down of the appropriation so that we should know of any radical changes that were made in certain of the many activities he found it necessary to review in his annual statement. We are given two lines in the estimates of the Depatment of Munitions and Supply, and page after page in all the other departments.
My next criticism is this. While it may be quite true that the function of the Department of Munitions and Supply is to purchase on order what is requisitioned by other branches of the services, not only in Canada but abroad, now that we are in the fifth year of the war does the committee really think that is sufficient at this stage? Do you really think, Mr. Chairman, that we are taking a sufficiently long-range view in having this department responsible for all munitions and supply, construction and so on, -without some definite planning for the future? I realize at once that the task of the minister is of great magnitude; but to my mind it is not planning for the future with respect to -many branches 
of the services, some of which I shall recite in a few moments. In the meantime the general criticism I have to make is that the minister's statement seems to resolve itself into an historical review of what has been done. We have that review in the press from day to day, from week to week, and from month to month; we have it in the publications of the wartime information board and in other sources of information. They tell us of the increase in production here and there when it is all gathered together. It should not be necessary for the minister to occupy the time of the committee in giving us another historical review of what is happening.
The assets held by the crown are now very large. With the holding of the assets there comes the responsibility of keeping them at work, particularly the capital assets. If there is not sufficient work for those plants in supplying munitions, then some department of government should be responsible for seeing to it that the capital expenditure is kept operating on peace-time needs, if not on wartime needs. It may be said that it is quite easy to shut down a few plants and transfer the employees, but you cannot transfer the fixed assets. Someone should be giving consideration to that particular part of our programme. The war targets have been attained, and in attaining them, considerable programme revision has been found necessary. That is inevitable. But in the revision which is necessary on account of change in types and kinds of war machines, the shutting-down of plants is something which should be given more consideration.
Single-purpose plants have been referred to. I can realize the difficulty of transforming them into something which is necessary on a larger scale. The probability is that the single-purpose plants are small and perhaps located in small communities where labour conditions are such that there is not sufficient labour to justify any other course. Yet there is a crying need in Canada to-day for peacetime industries in small communities where industries are now working partly on war production. These industries are necessary to the economic life of Canada. They are necessary to keep the population in the small towns. Small single-purpose plants should be kept in operation so that the small centres across Canada will not be disorganized. Through the enthusiasm- and encouragement of the munitions industry in days gone by, many of these small industries have become established. They are no longer necessary. They find that they will have to leave the 'town, and when peace is declared we are apt to have the spectacle of ghost towns springing up

War Appropriation-Supplies
all across Canada. Up to a short time ago there were thriving munitions industries in those towns. Let us take time by the forelock. Let some department of government take the responsibility of planning now with regard to the single-purpose plants referred to by the minister, and keep them in some kind of production.
It is not enough to cooperate with national selective service and move the population from point to point. Consideration must be given to the plants themselves. The increase of fifty per cent in aircraft production is something which I think ought to arouse the Canadian people who are now air-minded, and I would say that it is in the interests of Canada. The export production that we have had-"L for lanky", I think they call it over the radio- all helps, it is quite true, to build up the morale of the Canadian people. Congratulations were extended to the minister on this production, and they were quite in order, but let us have all sides of the picture as we go along. I did not hear very much said about the casualties in Ortona being taken to hospital in jeeps because no ambulances were available. It is a great tribute to the Canadian people that our trucks and ambulances can get through the sands of Africa, but there are other places where matters could be improved considerably. It is very nice to hear the minister tell us of these tributes that have been paid to us, but I should like him to present something more 'forward looking.
In the matter of mechanical transport we learn that our production has been 593,000 units, but now we find that this department has also gone into the business of supplying freight cars and engines for domestic use. If that is just a case of helping out because the Department of Munitions and Supply has under its control the equipment and tools necessary to make these things, well and good, but let that production go back into its natural channels, and let those who are able to build that equipment do so, as soon as possible.
Then I understand that the production of explosives has been reduced to some extent, and that one plant has been shut down. I wonder why that should be the case. I am trying to follow the minister's remarks seri-iatim, but he mentioned explosives in the early part of his remarks and dealt with chemicals later on, while the hon. member for Peterborough West raised the question of glycerine. I wonder why within the last month the glycerine market should have slumped. I wonder why there should be no sale for crude glycerine in Canada to-day. I congratulate the government upon holding the ceiling price of glycerine at 12i cents a pound, in contrast with the situation in the last war when, because of
world conditions, it soared to three or four times that price. The market price now, however, is down to around nine cents, with no sales. I think the parliamentary assistant should give the committee the story of that commodity, which is a natural product of Canada, because I am sure the present price will have far-reaching effects in connection with the raw material which goes to make up that product. In this country, which has very few plants able to handle crude glycerine, I wonder if there is not something going on between those plants, just to hold down the market, or if there is some other reason. I think in fairness to Canada the minister or his parliamentary assistant should give a frank statement as to the reserve supply of this commodity.
We were told that gun production has seen some conversion carried out, but we have no details. Probably the minister has not time in one statement to go into everything, but we are interested in details. I am sure Canada would be greatly interested to learn that we are working on orders for China, and also that there is another type of naval gun coming. Similarly in connection with small arms we have a modified version of the Bren gun. The minister mentioned that two cordite plants had been closed and that the plant at Nobel had been discontinued, so that the remarks I made previously in that regard are borne out by this part of the minister's statement. Tribute was paid to our chemists, chemical engineers and engineers. I join in that tribute modestly, perhaps, because I happen to be one of them, though I do not work at that profession, which has been long neglected. It is not recognized as a profession as we understand them, but I should like to take advantage of this occasion to say that it should be so recognized. No other country in the world has the opportunity Canada has for the development of chemical and engineering research, owing to the natural resources with which this dominion is blessed; and nothing that can be done to raise the standard of that profession should be left undone. Anything that will tend to increase the research carried on in Canada will work to the benefit of this country. The minister mentioned that he had fifty units working on explosives of one kind and another. It is hardly enough to say just that. How many of these units are operating; how many are closed down, and where are they located? Has the manufacturing industry of Canada been advised through the proper channels that it is not likely some of these institutions will commence operations again? Has any survey been made to ascertain what might be done with the units that are closed down?

I come now to the portion of the minister's remarks dealing with construction, including that in connection with air training schools and barracks. If I heard the minister aright, $100,000,000 is to be devoted to this type of construction during the coming year. I wonder whether we are looking forward to what will happen when the war is over, and whether we we are taking any care to see that these undertakings, which represent a tremendous investment, are located near centres where they will be of some use after the war. I think too many heavy expenditures have been made on construction, and fairly good construction at that, in remote parts of Canada when it was not absolutely necessary to have these buildt-ings so far removed from centres of population. This country is now filled with the idea that we are to raise a new brand of youth, that we are to have youth training centres, and that many of these buildings will be used for cadet training centres and1 physical culture centres of one kind or another. Many of these buildings would come in very handy and be very useful in connection with the housing and training of our youth when peace returns. We cannot stop this youth movement; they are going to demand the use of these facilities, and in the expenditures made from now on consideration should be given to these factors when deciding where these buildings should be located. A good many of us are of the opinion that this war will end in tw'o or three years, if not before, and that then we shall have a great surge of boys returning, with a great demand1 for facilities of this kind.
I am thinking of one instance which comes forcefully to mind at the moment, and perhaps I might pass it on to the minister. We have about eight sea cadet corps training in the basements and gymnasiums of schools in the city of Toronto. There are no facilities for what they call a deck, on which these boys can train as sea cadets. When the war is over we shall still be training sea cadets, not only in Ontario but in. other parts of Canada. In Malvern collegiate institute we are training air cadets. There are no proper facilities at that school for the training of these boys. When the war is over we shall still be training air cadets. If we had some centre that could be used for that particular purpose we would avoid interfering with the school curriculum and would build up a centre of training to which the youth, of this country might go. Pupils do not like to go back to school after hours; if they do, when they are there they do not feel that they have a home of their own. So that in the construction programme in all parts of Canada I hope consideration will be given to having these buildings erected in or near centres of population.

For the first time I realized more of what the Department of Munitions and Supply was doing when I found that it was asked to provide, I presume for war and other plants, social, educational and health schemes, and I think the minister said baby clinics and other things that might come under a health programme. My general criticism of a programme of this kind is based on the fact that we have permanent health programmes, carried on in permanent structures in the municipalities. We have permanent programmes and permanent construction fostered by the provinces. We have another set of temporary structures or temporary services for these plants. Some department of government should be charged with the responsibility of synchronizing these particular efforts. A great difficulty with our form of government is that Jones does not know what Smith is doing. I venture the opinion that in the carrying out of the social and health and educational schemes recited by the minister there is very little coordination or coalescence between the present set-up and the different organizations set up in the provinces to render these services.
The same thing can be said about the handling of medical stores. In Ottawa there is a medical stores branch for the army and I understand they indent upon Munitions and Supply. The Minister of Pensions and National Health has a very good centre for the dispensing of standard medicines, a centre which has been built up over the last twenty years, a centre which is functioning very well. The navy, the senior service, has its own orders of the day with regard to these supplies, but I cannot say whether they indent upon Munitions and Supply. However, they do their own distributing in their own way. The air force has another system set up. The result is that there are four or .five systems with four or five sets of personnel. The army, the air force and the navy have men mixing up pharmaceuticals of one* kind or another and receiving army, air force or navy pay. The Department of Pensions and National Health have a civilian staff doing the same thing and receiving civilian pay. The difference between the rates of pay is such that proper cooperation in this work is not obtained. To a large extent the men charged with the responsibility of doing this work in the ariny, the navy or the air force are lieutenants or other commissioned officers who have a smattering of the subject, perhaps learned in a back-country drugstore. They are not trained in the manufacturing of pharmaceuticals, with the result that there is not the

War Appropriation-Supplies
efficiency there would be if a proper plan were adopted and there were more coordination of these efforts.
There is a point I should like to make in connection with the health centre programme being sponsored by the minister's department. Take Kingston, for instance, where I understand a centre is located. I think it will be found that the government centre is competing with other like establishments for the necessary labour. I notice the parliamentary assistant is making a note. If Kingston is not the right place, then these remarks will apply to other places. As I say, I believe it will be found that the government centre is competing with other organizations for the personnel to carry on electro-therapy work and other work needed in the centre.
I come now to the matter of controls. The minister says that there are seventeen controllers. That may be right, but there must be about 1,700 deputy controllers. According to the correspondence I have had the privilege of looking over, there seems to be a different signature on every letter. I note with interest the statement of the minister that some of these controls are not now necessary. These controllers should be released as quickly as possible, because I think it will be found that while perhaps they have not irritated industry in general, they have made it quite difficult for industry to carry on. Now that inventories are piling up in Munitions and Supply, more and more consideration should be given to relaxing these controls. I do not want to take the responsibility for this, should there be a substantial relaxing of these controls and then by some misadventure election time comes along and this be taken as another plank in the platform of my hon. friends who sit opposite. That plank is already in the platform of the party it is my pleasure to support.
We are still importing tremendous quantities of coal. The minister stated that providence was kind to us this year but conditions may be serious next year. We must take the long-range view of this and build up a reserve stock of fuel for next year. Reference has been made to the tendency of industry to centralize itself. Some long-range scheme should be adopted, whereby industry could be transferred closer to the supply of coal, particularly to points in western Canada. As the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has said at different times, more industries should be established where coal is available. Not only would that help in the distribution of fuel, but the effect upon the labour supply would bo considerable. This year industry in
Winnipeg was able to get labour. This year industry in Toronto was not able to get labour. We all know that labour is available during the winter months in western Canada and, as I say, plans should be made to transfer as much industry as possible to this part of Canada.
The minister referred to anthracite coal and substitutes for anthracite coal. Pocahontas coal is the principal substitute for anthracite coal. It has done a good1 job in this last winter which has been quite mild, but what has happened is that fifty-seven varieties of Pocahontas coal are being offered to the consumers. The quality depends upon the amount of other grades, mostly lower, of coal that are mixed in.
I come now to the question of lumber. Four or five billion board feet have been produced and the exports have amounted to one billion board feet. Referring particularly to planks and boards, I wonder if the crown companies need to exercise as much control? Do they need to go into this business as intensely as they are doing? I do not know and I ask the minister to have his parliamentary assistant answer this question: Can we not do away with much of the control exercised over this particular industry and let it carry on naturally?
I should like to say a word about plywoods and veneers. As time goes on there will be a tremendous increase in the use of these woods in all parts of the world. I ask whatever minister has the responsibility in this matter to give a close study to the possible development of plywoods and veneers. These woods have made tremendous strides during the war and I am sure they will make greater strides after the war is over. They are replacing steel and aluminum and many other lighter metals in a great many ways.
I come now to the base metals. Perhaps we have heard enough about aluminum and we have a fairly good idea about the amount of production. On the whole Canada is doing a good job in producing aluminum. Whether or not the structure which makes it possible for the plant to operate is properly organized is a question upon which I am not going to touch. But I wonder why we are not producing more magnesium. This metal is lighter than aluminum. In many ways it is better than aluminum, but in other ways it has certain handicaps to overcome. I ask the minister or the parliamentary assistant to give the committee a frank statement on the magnesium situation. Why are we producing only thirteen tons a day? While the hon member is making a note, perhaps he will permit me to make another comment. Is

War Appropriation-Supplies
the reason for this small production of magnesium the fact that we have such a tremendous productive capacity of aluminum? Is it that we do not want to interfere in any way with the sale of aluminum or with the position of this metal after the war? My comments are based on general observations.
At Thetford Mines, asbestos mines, I imagine I would be safe in saying that there are lying at the pit-head and not being used thousands of tons of semi-dressed magnesium ores, bereft of their mica and asbestos and broken into sizes which could readily be handled by steam shovel or otherwise, with perhaps one-third of the 'work of dressing already done on them. This is not being used and there is no particular development of any consequence apart from the thirteen tons a day which the minister mentioned. I should like to have a statement from the minister, if it is within the ambit of his department, as to why we are not using more magnesium and why more development work is not being done on this natural resource which we have in our country in such abundance.
As to molybdenum, copper and the other base metals, my understanding is that we have a tremendous backlog of copper and I think that should be maintained.
While copper is in an easy position, there is no great stock-pile.

There is no great stock-pile, the minister says. Then now is the time to get a stock-pile, because we are having some difficulty in holding the price of copper in world markets. If that is the case, it must be in production at a substantial profit, and certainly we should have on hand a fair supply of this essential material.
We are all disappointed that over the last twenty years there has been no definite or positive development of the tar sands, and I hope the hon. member for Davenport will pursue his quest with the department with regard to this particular development.
The interesting statement given by the minister on the rubber situation will be pleasing to the Canadian people. I should like to know whether the men who are responsible for that development, the engineers, chemists and what-not, are being given proper recognition. It is interesting to know that our production of steel in Canada has progressed in the proportions it has during the last decade. We are still importing one-third of our requirements. That strikes me as a very small figure, because I was of the opinion that we were importing more. I should like the minister to put on record the figures of 
our imports of steel. At the same time I wish to emphasize this warning to those hon. members who have the idea that the tape on the border between the United States and Canada is going to be rolled up-the tape being the duties at present in being and not now being applied-what will happen to the steel industry when the war is over if their policy is followed right through? How long should we be in the position of importing only one-third of our requirements and producing the other two-thirds? That is something which should give Canada serious concern, when we think of all the employees who are now engaged in the manufacture of steel in this country. I should like the minister or his parliamentary assistant to put on the record the number of workers now engaged in the steel industry in Canada.
Then I come to trucks. We are not producing them. The transit controller has put a control on trucks so that they will not be worn out too fast. As long as trucks are needed in the European theatre of war, let us do without them and devote our production of trucks to war purposes. But if the transit controller, working in harmony with other branches of the Department of Munitions and Supply, finds it necessary to restrict the use of trucks in this country, let me just bring to the attention of hon. members one little problem in that connection. The trucking hours have been staggered. Those of us who are operating trucks will put up with any inconvenience that may be necessary because there is a war on; but when the controller goes farther and passes regulations that trucks shall not operate on a certain day of the week, shall be off the highway one day in five-and with Saturday afternoon off, that brings the number of days operations to four -I want to say that the industry finds great difficulty in providing other work for the truck drivers to do on the day when they cannot take out their machines. Someone might say, put them in some other line of production. But truck drivers get a premium of from five to six or ten cents an hour over the average factory labourer. Moreover, the truck driver is out in the weather four days in the week, and he does not like going into the shop on the fifth day and then having to go back out into the weather the next day. His constitution will not stand it. When he does go into the shop he will not accept the pay which the ordinary labourer is drawing, and the ordinary labourer -and the truck driver may not be as efficient because he is working inside only one day a week-is not satisfied to work alongside him for from five to ten cents an hour less.

But the minister mentioned the transit controller and staggered hours.
The transit controller has to do with transporting people in buses and street-cars.

That is on the record anyway, and he that hath charge and responsibility therefor, let him note and pay heed to that I have said.
In the main my criticism is that there is no department of government that is forwardlooking with regard to this tremendous industrial asset which we have found it necessary to build up to produce munitions of war, not only with regard to the asset in its capital sense but with regard to the future vocations for men and women engaged in this industry across the country. What are you going to do with them when hostilities cease? What are you going to do now with the people engaged in those portions of the industry which are closing down, with, consequent moving from place to place? What are you going to do with the municipalities who find that these war industries have left them? That is something which is the responsibility of this house and something to which considerable thought should be given. When I say that, I am not anxious that the Department of Munitions and Supply should assume the whole responsibility for the future of that great personnel now earning their living from this war-time necessity. But these workers do need to be guided and to be told that something is likely to happen to the industry in which they are engaged, and some lead should be given to them as to where they are to be able to earn their living. It is easy enough to say that the housewives can go back to their homes and the schoolboys and schoolgirls go back to school, but that is not enough. Many of' the housewives will never go back to domestic duties. A great number of the schoolboys and schoolgirls will not go back to school. Something more has to be done, and when that something more is being done for them I should like to see them guided1 by these ten good points which I ran across in a newspaper to-day, reprinted from the Land o' Lakes News, in the San Francisco Argonaut:
1.	You cannot bring about prosperity by discouraging thrift.
2.	You cannot strengthen the weak by weakening the strong.
3.	You cannot help small men by tearing down big men.
4.	You cannot help the poor by destroying the rich.
5.	You cannot lift the wage-earner by pulling down the wage-payer.
6.	You cannot keep out of trouble by spending more than your income.
7.	You cannot further the brotherhood of man by inciting class hatred.
8.	You cannot establish sound security on borrowed money.
9.	You cannot build character and courage by taking away a man's initiative and independence.
10.	You cannot help men permanently by doing for them what they could and should do for themselves.
But we can guide them and make a frank statement to them of the position into which we are drifting, and some department of government, in cooperation with, the Department of Munitions and Supply, should be charged with the responsibility of. taking a forwardlooking view in. the position in. which we now find ourselves.

In entering upon a discussion of the estimates of the Department of Munitions and Supply, I have in mind the numerous restrictions placed on the manufacture of articles of which the civilian population of this country has an essential need. At a time when farmers must renew their agricultural implements the all-essential farming industry is deprived of indispensable machines. The producers of maple sugar and syrup are in a similarly deplorable situation as regards their maple groves. We are told that metals are reserved for the prosecution of war. When it is obvious that war profiteers have exported thousands of tons of Canadian metal to the enemy since the declaration of war and a few days only before the outbreak of the conflict, is it surprising that our essential civilian industries should be deprived of articles necessary for their production? We are told again and again by the government that metals are reserved for the prosecution of war. Then, why did they authorize the export of our metals to Japan, a few weeks before war started between that country and the United States and Canada hastened to declare war on her? Is it conceivable that the government of Canada should have shown so little foresight as to let the enemy use our metals for building up a war machine which has already caused deaths within the ranks of our army, our navy and our air force? Those who have been responsible for such a dire situation shall be required by the people to account for their rank carelessness. I cannot find words strong enough to stigmatize such an attitude. I may be told that "such a situation could not have been anticipated". That is a poor excuse. The premonitory signs of Japan's warlike intentions could not

War Appropriation-Supplies

have escaped the attention of the government. Their connection with the Rome-Berlin axis was obvious. Reference to Hansard will show the concern of the government about the action of Japan, many months before her attack against Pearl Harbor. Once again, criminal purveyors had succeeded in cheating the authorities in order to increase their wealth. A small number of profiteers were waxing rich in betraying their country and laying our soldiers, airmen and sailors open to the attacks of the warships, bombers, guns and machine guns built by the enemy out of our metals. Such is the treacherous work of loathsome exporters and manufacturers who should be treated as the worst felons and brought before the courts of justice to answer for their crime.
I shall now deal with the rationing of oils and gasoline. It was indeed worth while to resort to it. It has been and is still disastrous. We have seen holders of the lowest category of ration books travel by motor car during the summer, the fall and even the winter. The black market was rampant for gasoline as well as for all rationed goods, meats, foodstuffs, sugar, alcohol, and so forth.
In a country like ours, endowed with enormous natural resources, rationing is not only a nonsense but an utter folly. As evidence, I need only mention the wasting of millions of pounds of meat, recently revealed, the hoarding, by thousands of families, of foodstuffs definitely wasted because they have become unfit for consumption and the failure of the government to carry out their now famous planned economy programme. That is a meaningless term.
In fact, the government, panic-stricken before the condition it has brought about, has just lifted restrictions on meat and beer. Believe me, it will not stop at that, all the more since it is now vainly trying to coax itself back into the favour of the people before appealing to the country, which step is required by public censure and the constitution.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) remarked last Friday, in the course of the debate, on the ruinous competition maintained by our railways with regard to transportation all over the country. This is a well-known fact. The Canadian National Railways, however, are ready to build a new elevated railroad in the northern part of Montreal instead of using the Canadian Pacific track over a long stretch of the new branch-line. Elevated railroads in 1944! Are they so little conscious of progress and reality that they must cut up six of the lovliest parishes of Montreal to make them reek with evil smells?
TMr. Lanombe.]
Let the government reject such a proposal. If new railroads are to be built, let them be underground. If this should cost ten or fifteen million dollars extra, little does it matter. A country which subscribes bounteous gifts and billion dollar presents annually can afford to spend a few million dollars on constructive and permanent works.
Let us think of the post-war period and save the northern part of Montreal from the calamity of elevated railroads which would shame the present government and disgrace the metropolis of Canada.

speechtext: I have given my ruling and I would ask the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains to be kind enough to accept it and resume his seat. I know 'he realizes that he is out of order.
I accept youT ruling, Mr. Chairman, but I shall speak on this subject at some future date.

First I wish to refer to the sale of surpluses of equipment from barracks, camps and so on, and surpluses of raw materials, by the War Assets Corporation. This is a very important matter and one upon which the people of Canada have, I believe, the right to an assurance from the government that in the operation of the War Assets Corporation the sales that take place shall be open to inspection by the public as a whole. To date we have had no assurance in this regard. Tens if not hundreds of millions of dollars of surplus goods, war goods and the like, will be available for sale. There will be sales from time to time as surpluses accumulate and these will continue until the end of the war and after.
A committee has been set up in order to ascertain the materials, and a corporation has been set up in order to dispose of those materials. In order to reassure all the people of the country that there will be equality of opportunity and of consideration, the transactions should be< conducted in the open. In that, I have support in the stand that is being taken in the United States.
The minister is aware of the steps that are being taken there. Two outstanding members were appointed by the administration to look into the matter and make recommendations, and they did so. I could deal with these particular points individually, but instead of doing so I am going to quote from the records of the War and Post-war Adjustment Policy report to the United States congress in order to ascertain whether or not similar principles are to be applied in Canada.
The basic principles accepted there, and applicable to Canada by reason of the similarity of conditions under which we live and the fact that we are joined together in common defence, are these. First, sell as much as can be early, without unduly disrupting normal trade; and second, no sales and no rentals to speculators, and none to promoters.
If this corporation is to operate fairly and squarely, that principle above all must be applied; otherwise we shall find ourselves in 100-108J
the position where speculators will take advantage of the fact that the government is in the market for the disposal of surplus goods, and the speculator rather than the government will reap the benefit.
Sell as in a gold-fish bowl, with records always open to public inspection. That to me is a most important recommendation. It is, I believe, one on which the minister should give his assurance at this time, the assurance in other words that what is to be done shall not be done behind closed doors or under the provisions of orders in council. Up to the present time, in the production of these goods and in the investigation into their costs, the people of Canada have not been able to secure full information. In the investigation of these matters in the war expenditures committee the people have been denied information. The same excuses for secrecy do not apply to the sales of such surpluses.
Next:
As far as practicable, use the same regular channels of trade that private business would m disposing of the particular properties.
No government operation of surplus war plants in competition with private industry.
I know there has been an exception made to that in Canada. There will be after the war in the rubber corporation at Sarnia, Ontario.
With what does that compete?
It is a government operation.
With what private industry does it compete?
It does not compete in the matter of manufacture, true enough, but it is actually the first move along the road to socialization.

It is a wholly non-competitive industry.
Mr. DIEFENBAKER.: That is true.
Its product will compete.
With what?
Other manufacturers.
There is no manufacturer of rubber in this country.
The production of rubber that goes on the market.

They do not manufacture
rubber.

This is one industry that we know about to-day that is to be operated by the government after the war.

Its course will be that of public ownership, something that the government has invariably stood opposed to. I should like to ask the minister whether it is the intention, after the war is over, to operate surplus war plants in Canada in opposition to private business. The minister says that so far as the Polymer Corporation is concerned, for the time being it is not operating in opposition to private business in the manufacture of rubber. That is true; but will he give the assurance that after the war it is not the intention of the government to operate any of the surplus industries in opposition to private industry?
I might answer that now. This government has, as far as I know since I have been a member of it, never entered into the manufacture of anything competitive with private industry.
That is not the question. Is it the intention in so far as surplus war plants are concerned, or any of them, to operate them by the state in competition with private industry?
The government's policy will be made known in due course.

That is exactly the point. The minister was very quick to answer that the government had not done it before the war, but he is not so fast on the trigger in so far as the post-war plans of the government are concerned in this connection.

According to my hon. friend his party is most hopeful of operating the government immediately after the war. Did he ever announce a plan for that purpose? If he has it has been to the Kiwanis club or some stock-breeders' association, not to the house.

Speaking about
stock-breeders' associations and the like, I think the minister had better get together with other ministers over there. In November or December of last year the minister announced that in the post-war period there was one matter that we must all be sure about, namely that we must take a definite stand that there shall be no unnecessary public works in order to guard against unemployment. On the same day that the minister was making his speech in Toronto the Minister of Pensions and National Health said that one thing we must do after the war in order to ensure that there will not be unemployment is to engage in a very wide public works programme. The ministers did not agree during the same day that they were enunciating a post-war programme. I would point out that I have not yet received an answer to the

question as to whether or not it is the intention of this government to operate any industries after the war in opposition to private enterprise.
With regard to the disposal of surplus the United States have adopted as a recommended principle that there shall be:
No monopoly; equal access to surpluses for all businesses; preference to local ownership, but no subsidizing of one part of the country against another.
That, too, is an important matter, and one upon which the committee and the country have the right to expect the assurance of the minister. We who come from the prairie provinces and the maritimes realize that during the period of the war no real and fair opportunity has been given to the building up of industries that could have been built up in those sections. In the disposal of those surpluses are those parts of Canada that were neglected during the war to receive an equality of opportunity in the securing of the surpluses that are disposed of between now and the end of the war and following the end of the war?
May I go on from there with something else upon which we require information in regard to surpluses? We should like a statement from the minister now or at some time during this debate as to the value of the tremendous amounts of supplies that lie piled up along the right of way between Ontario and the maritimes, much of which has been there for a very long period of time.
No.
That is what we want information on. How many million dollars worth of stuff-
Why does the hon. member not ask a question instead of making statements that are not correct?

The statements I make are correct, and I am asking for information as to particulars of the amount. I ask the minister how many million dollars worth of stuff has been on the right of way for a period of three years? How many million dollars worth of stuff has been there for two years? What is being done in connection with the salvaging of this stuff piled along the right of way?
I can answer that question now. No millions have been there for three years and no millions have been there for two years.

Has the minister the figures as to the value of the stuff that has been on the right of way for three years?

Yes. There has been none.

The minister makes that statement; therefore he must have the particulars. I am asking the minister to produce the particulars showing the value of the stuff on the right of way that has fallen into poor condition and is unusable because it has been there for such a long time. The minister says that there is none.

Mr. Chairman, I
had just about concluded the question I desired to ask the minister. What I have asked in connection with the War Assets Corporation might be epitomized in one question, namely: is the principle of the goldfish bowl to be applied as far as the disposal of surpluses is concerned? The matter is of very great interest in the business world in general. In the disposal of office equipment, kitchen equipment, stoves and the like, for instance, when the various air schools are closed up, will the general public have an opportunity to purchase needed supplies? Will the sales be made openly, so that all may have an opportunity to replenish their own requirements, which have been reduced to a minimum during the period of war?
I mentioned the situation with regard to the supplies that were piled up along the right of way of the various railways of this country. A portion of those supplies has been moved during the past year. Has that portion been moved overseas, or has it been transferred elsewhere for storage or disposal?
In that connection I should like to ask a question in reference to certain types of armoured equipment and the like. Have many of these vehicles been found no longer necessary and not required for overseas use by reason of changed war conditions and, if so, what disposition has been made of them? In particular, were any of the four-wheel drive vehicles known as "quads" not required overseas, or found unfit for service; if so, how many were involved and what disposition has been made of them. Also in reference to the production of Heath-Robinson lorries, how many of those were produced; were they found unfit for service and, if so, what was done with them after that was ascertained? I' ask for information for the purpose of finding out what disposition is being made of
these armaments or supplies which are not to be shipped overseas by reason of changed conditions.
I should like to request some information in regard to the demobilization of war industry. I think the minister should now be in a position to give the country a picture of what is in mind in that regard. To-day he pointed out the changes that have taken place, the manner in which the production of certain munitions and implements of war has been reduced, and so on. When that production finally ceases, naturally some factories will be closed down. What are the plans for the use of those factories in the transition period between war and peace? What are the plans for the sale or disposal of those plants? For instance, during the past three and a half to four years a phenomenal record has been made under the empire air training scheme. Some of those schools are now being closed. What does the government propose to do with the buildings located at those schools? Does it intend to turn them over to the municipalities to be used as, hospitals and similar institutions? As yet no plan has been placed before this, house, and I should like to have from the minister something of the general design or pattern the government has in mind, not the details but the general scheme for demobilization of war industry, both during the period of war as changing conditions make that necessary and after the war is over.
There is one other matter, and I think the minister would be the one through whom that information should be made available. What is the plan of the government in regard to the demobilization of economic controls, under the planned economy which has been in effect during the war? To what extent is it intended gradually to remove these uneconomic controls, or at least a portion of them? In the United States, in the United Kingdom, plans are being made and announced; parliament is being taken into the confidence of the ministry. So far as we in this house are concerned, however, plans of that kind have not been placed before us. I mentioned economic controls; I would add the departure from parliamentary government. It is time that we knew how long it is intended to continue the present trend. Only yesterday I received an answer to a question 'which indicates how parliament is being by-passed by those who to-day in the main control the economy of this country. I refer to the matter of orders in council. It is an amazing record that from the beginning of the war until March 15, 1944, there should be 42,398 orders in council passed, as well as 23,287 minutes of treasury board. I do not object to orders in council between
War Appropriation-Supplies

sessions, in the interests of efficiency, effectiveness and immediate action. This session commenced on January' 27 and from that date to March 15 a total of 1,186 orders in council and 850 minutes of treasury board were passed. While parliament has sat, parliament has not legislated. That function has been performed outside of this chamber.
These are matters removed from partisan consideration although, when they are brought before parliament, too often the attitude is taken that they are partisan matters. I ask the minister to take parliament and the country into his confidence. We have had in the course of the last few weeks a general picture of the demobilization of man-power after the war. We should now have revealed to us the story of the plans for the' demobilization of war industry. Parliament and the people are entitled to a better answer than the one I got from the minister this afternoon when I asked him whether the government intended to operate industry in opposition to private enterprise after the war; the answer being that the government policy would be revealed in due course. We get answers in this parliament such as, "Government policy will be revealed in due course," and, "It is not in the public interest," and that sort of thing. We are entitled to the fullest information and we should not be given answers of that kind. The other day, when a question was asked as to what salaries are paid to officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the answer was given that it would not be in the public interest to give this information because it would reveal to private industry details with regard to government. Answers like that are not good enough.
Unless plans are made now, unless we know the scheme, there will be chaos when peace comes. We are not asking the minister to give the picture in detail; all we want is an outline of what the government intends to act on. I have not overlooked the fact that there does not seem to be agreement as to post-war plans, even among the ministry. One said that he believed in the principle of public works during the transition period and the other stated in effect that the principle of public works is something that , should be frowned upon. There seems to be disagreement in the government, disagreement among the ministers as to post-war planning. Let us have the picture, let us know what the post-war plans are for the demobilization of industry to which $800,000,000 have been advanced in the way of capital assistance, for unless plans are made now there will be complete chaos in carrying out this demobilization.

Mr. Chairman, I am not
going to make a speech but I wish to state a couple of facts. I always enjoy listening to the Iron, member (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has just taken his seat, but I do not look at things just in the way he does. He has stated that over 1,100 orders in council have been passed, but we must not forget that if each one of those orders had been brought before this house and all the members of the Social Credit and the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and a good percentage of the Conservative members had spoken, we would not be out of here in twelve months. Those orders in council w'ere authorized by parliament and they were absolutely necessary. I know that special information has been withheld, but when the general public are not asking for it I do not just see why we should give special information that may not be good for them.
When I was a young lad I read about the pioneers who settled in Ontario, in Manitoba and throughout the west. I do not think there has been a truer pioneer in Canada, either in the past or present, than the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). It would not be hard to prove that statement. All we have to do is to consider what he has done, the new things he has introduced', sometimes against opposition. Tanks were never made in Canada before. Just consider the programme that was outlined on Friday last in connection with Trans-Canada Air Lines. He is one of the greatest pioneers that have ever occupied, a seat in this house or in any provincial house in Canada.
As I listened to the minister this afternoon my imagination began to work and I could see hundreds of thousands of workers doing the things that have been planned by the minister to be done. The minister held out for collective bargaining long before that w'as considered by the general public; also holidays with pay. He was a real pioneer. Another things that stands out is the fact that there has not been one dollar of graft in connection wuth the war effort. If any one says that that is not a real achievement when one is dealing with human nature of all kinds, then he had better go back and think again. Let us look at what happened. I know we have a committee on war expenditures; I know what their duties are; but when any one has been suspected of padding a payroll or carrying on any funny work the Minister of Munitions and Supply has immediately called in the Department of Justice; the mounted police investigate and a court action may follow. The minister does not get any-

War Appropriation-Supplies
thing out of these things except criticism. That is very poor politics, but is doughty statesmanship on his part and he is becoming more popular than ever.
We at the head of the lakes think there are few men like the Minister of Munitions and Supply. This week I received a number of letters asking why I did not rise in my place and state that the minister is above reproach. He is above reproach. Whether you belong to our group or to any other I am sure you will agree with me when I express the hope that he may be long spared to us. He learned to use the square and compass when he was a boy, and he is still using them. No matter what happens, under his control there will be neither chaos nor tumult.

The war has caused an expansion in our national industry which might be termed magical.. In this conflict which has lasted for almost five years Canada has become the arsenal of the united nations. In order to attain this end the Department of Munitions and Supply has had, since its inception in September, 1939, to organize a vast system of production, create (he necessary factories and spend many millions of dollars for these purposes.
The county of Terrebonne has had the privilege of cooperating very closely with this war production. The towns of Terrebonne, Ste. Jerome and St. Therese have been almost exclusively engaged in war production and they have cooperated in a sustained and loyal effort. The Bouchard plants, located at Ste. Therese, were built for the purpose of filling shells and other essential purposes, and they are rated among the most important war industries, not only in Canada but in the whole empire. The municipal councils, the public bodies and the chamber of commerce of Ste. Therese, together with the municipal councils of Terrebonne and of Ste. Anne des Plaines, gave the Allied War Supplies Corporation in the foundation of Bouchard and its branches a support which could be used as a model for the rest of the country. The working class of my county-one of the most industrious of the country-even if it insisted upon its right of belonging to unions in order to protect its privileges, has nevertheless always shown a will to cooperate which denotes its social sense and its progressive spirit. There were no strikes in my county and in its factories. I wish to point that out because it honours my constituents.
Nobody was more closely related than myself to the creation and development of the Bouchard plants. I gave my best cooperation because I was conscious that in so doing I was,
as a member, serving the interests of my country. I sometimes objected to the wastefulness of Defence Industries Limited, because I knew I was right. The companies entrusted with the war production are often seriously to blame; they believe they are authorized to spend freely and without general planning; they form, in the midst of their directorates, family compacts which are rejected and hated by the working classes; they are often unfair when they choose their labourers. Quite often it happens that simply because a skilled worker does not speak English well enough, he is replaced by another who speaks English only. This is very inconsistent, since most of the workers in the Quebec war factories are French Canadians. It also happens too often that employees are fired, forsooth, because they are suddenly found inefficient after two or three years' service, and they are replaced by people from Nobel or Winnipeg, who speak only one language and whose evident inefficiency is, in many cases, a cause for laughter and dissatisfaction among other employees.
I wish in' particular to protest, as member for Terrebonne, against the unfairness of Defence Industries Limited, the company in charge of the plants known as Bouchard, and located at Ste. Therese, in my constituency.
My remarks on this will be short. I consider this statement important, both for the information of this house and for the protection of the working classes of my province.
During the last three or four weeks Defence Industries Limited, at Bouchard, hired about fifty employees from its Nobel plant, in Ontario, to fill, not labourers' positions, but a number of controlling posts which had been occupied with efficiency for two or three years by French- and English-speaking Canadians residing in my county, in the Montreal district, and even throughout the province of Quebec. These employees were dismissed or were compelled to accept .secondary jobs. Who hired the employees at Nobel? Who ordered their transfer?
I have reason to believe that this transfer was effected without the knowledge of the Department of Munitions and Supply, even without the knowledge of the Department of Labour, which controls man-power. I am convinced, however, that Defence Industries Limited took advantage of the authorization which might be granted by the laws, or even granted to itself the right of transferring from one of its plants to another a certain group of employees, thus avoiding going through local or regional offices of the selective service, and thus attaining more easily its purposes of partisanship.
