I always like to listen to the hon. member for Fort William' (Mr. Mclvor), lauding the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). On occasions I have heard the hon. member place the minister in a rank seemingly higher than the hosts of heaven, so that I have had to tell him, "Be careful, Dan, you are almost sacrilegious." I am sure the minister often says to himself, "May the Lord save me from my friends."
I am going to try to give him this evening a picture of something to which he referred very briefly this afternoon-the oil sand area of Fort MeMurray, and let me, in turn, say, "0 Lord, save the minister from his friends in connection with what is going on up at Fort MeMurray."
I have been in contact for quite some time with the situation at Fort MeMurray. I did not go up last summer, for I did not want to be there when the initial programme was being entered into, but from what I have heard I am satisfied that it will be necessary to go next summer to see just how little has been done.
A few days ago the Edmonton Journal quoted a speech made in the Alberta legislature on March 14 by the Hon. Mr. Fallow, who is undoubtedly a responsible, conscientious gentleman-at least I believe him to be [DOT]-and in the course of his remarks he made some very strong statements. I am not sure how much the Minister of Munitions and Supply has to do with what is going on at Fort MeMurray. I hope it is little-
I may settle that now. I have nothing to do with it. The vote is in the Department of Mines and Resources. However, I like to hear my hon. friend explain these matters and I hope he will go ahead.

I was going to say I hope the minister had nothing to do with it because I think too much of him and I know his ability is too great to permit any such situation as is going on at Fort MeMurray to-day. Certainly the progress has not lived up to any of his expectations when he introduced the agreement approximately a year ago.
What did the hon. Mr. Fallow say? I will quote a few of his statements-and, I repeat, they are very strong statements coming from a minister of the crown:
Mr. Fallow charged that the northern undertaking has been a "colossal farce." War requirements for petroleum are so urgent that the dominion government has spent $1,700,000 in the past eighteen months to investigate the possibilities of extracting oil from the sand, i and so far as the actual investigation is con' cerned, all they have to show for it is a hole in the ground.

I know that hole in the ground was there before the contractors went north.
Out of the north came an endless procession of weird, incredulous stories of criminal incompetence and scandalous waste of public funds, and charges of sabotage were heard on every hand.
That is in keeping with correspondence I have had from Fort MeMurray, from people who would have no reason to state anything but the facts. Hon. Mr. Fallow goes on:
The stories I got from men who were working on the project made me wonder if the dominion government had borrowed some of the inmates of an insane asylum to handle the work.
And further:
No construction work was done that was not changed at least once, said the minister. Changes three to five times were not uncommon. It will perhaps be conservative to say that 25 per cent of the workmen were continuously engaged in tearing down some of what the other 75 per cent put up.
Further:
In summing up, Mr. Speaker, may I say that the pathetic flounderings of this gang of pussyfooting amateurs is beyond description.
That is very strong language. It is not my language, but it largely bears out what has been sent to me from Fort MeMurray.

Perhaps we had better
straighten that out now.
Will the minister allow me to continue my argument?
The hon. gentleman made a serious allegation.
I made no allegation; I quoted what a responsible minister said.
The hon. gentleman quoted it and therefore evidently endorsed it. It is strong language. He talks about amateurs; I want to give the pedigree of the people on both sides, including Mr. Fallow.
Will the minister take his seat and let me continue.

The hon. member is slandering
my associates.

The minister can say
anything he likes afterwards. I want to tell the minister he is altogether too combatant. He is too fond of arguing with anyone who says anything about his department. A few moments ago he said it was not his business but the business of the mines and resources department. Why then does he want to rise and interrupt my remarks?
May I continue where I left off a moment ago when I said that similar stories had come

War Appropriation-Supplies
to me. In January last I wrote to a friend in Edmonton to go to Fort McMurray and take photographs panoramic and I have in my hand the panoramic pictures he sent to me. They are dated January 25, 1944. I also have in my hand a photograph I took in 1942, for I have been to Fort McMurray on three different occasions. I do not talk about anything I do not see, and I am one of the few members who have been there. Last fall when certain gentlemen appeared before the reconstruction committee to testify in connection with this matter of the tar sandls. I did not know at the time that two of them had never been there, as I am informed, or I believe I would have asked that they retire. I am not sure that the third one was there. I am told that he was not, but he informed me that-he was and so I will take his word. There is too much long-distance talk with regard to a plant that is a long way off about which some who discuss it actually know little. I have here a picture of the plant which I took myself. It is a picture of the 1942 Abasand plant. That company should never have been displaced. That is my judgment and I will stack my judgment against anyone else's. I was in big business for many years, associated with engineers for a considerable time, and I will stack my business experience against anyone else's. Twenty-live years' experience of big business is not picked up in a few minutes.
This picture shows the oil sand mine. It shows the second or 1942 plant and I saw the plant operating, so that I know what it did, notwithstanding what anyone else may say. The 1944 picture does not show the big building to which the sand was taken out of the mine for separation. That building has been pulled down. The 1944 panoramic view shows that the 1942 separation building has been pulled down and it discloses the end of the first pulper. There were two. I am told on reliable authority-the officials of the Department of Mines and Resources can check up on this information-that that new building was started on a grade fifteen feet lower than it is to be. The foundations have been raised fifteen feet, the reason given being the fear that the Horse river would overflow and interfere with the pulping in the new building. I am told, what the Hon. Mr. Fallow said, that there have been numerous changes in construction. Every time a new manager comes, there is a change, and the minister knows there have been several of them. He shakes his head; then he does not know.

That is right; I have nothing to do with it.
100-109J

I am glad to hear that. I think too much of the minister to have him charged with such a mess as is reported there. It was about last May, I believe, that the first operators, or those who were directed to produce oil or asphalt at Fort McMurray, went there. Well, here is a picture taken in January, 1944. It shows the separator building is pulled down and some of the tanks have been moved across the river. The separating plant is down, not a thing done to the refinery. Nothing taken out of the pit in a year's time. What was done? A line of water-pipe is said to have been run all the way from that supposed townsite to the Athabaska river. It makes me laugh. It is being called a town-site. Apparently those who are in there expect to be able to build a town without proving anything as the minister intended should be done. Without anything being proved, a water-line has been run all the way to the Athabaska river. I am told that pipe was put into a trench eight feet deep and then taken out and laid on top of the ground. When the frost came along the pipe was put back in the trench again and covered with dirt. What a comedy! I just cannot find the right language to describe it. I am sure the minister would not have tolerated it for two seconds when he was in business building big elevators all over the country.
I have a number of little pictures here which show some fifteen or twenty bunkhouses or small houses being started. According to my information, of that number three perhaps are fit for occupation. No. 1 plumbing fixtures and a No. 1 heating plant have been put in the bunkhouse I slept in. When I was there, there was neither steam heat nor plumbing in it. I should have thought that the man on that job would have first followed out what the minister had planned. I am going to give the minister credit for this. The first thing he proposed to do was to make all the investigation possible and for that purpose $300,000 were appropriated. The first thing that should have been done was to prove something to the satisfaction of whoever was in charge there. That was not done. Money has, in my judgment, been squandered, wasted. That is borne out by what Mr. Fallow said. They are constructing buildings and there is nothing for anyone to do, because the mill is not up and will not be up soon. That is the last information I have and it is in accordance with the speech delivered by Mr. Fallow. The mill is not expected to be in operation before next fall.
The minister will remember that a year ago, in reading the agreement and giving the
War Appropriation-Supplies

talk on the production of the oil sands, he said that he expected that by the fall of 1943 the plant into which this country had poured a barrel of money would be in operation and making asphalt for the Alaska highway. Was that not right? Not a single, solitary thing has been made, not a drop of oil, not a pound of asphalt, because there is nothing in which to make it. I wish to protest' as strongly as I can, as a Canadian taxpayer, against such lack of business as is going on at Fort McMurray. I wish to protest as strongly as I pan against the waste, what appears to be the utter waste of public money. This is not Mr. Fallow saying that. I am saying it, and I am saying it on the basis of these pictures that I am looking at, which were taken on January 25, 1944, and if any of the press would like to have them I should like them to take them and publish them. For the expenditure of a barrel of money not a worthwhile thing has been done toward producing oil or asphalt. A few houses have been erected and a ditch or two dug. Some plumbing has been installed and perhaps a roadway patched up, but not a thing done for which the money was voted, namely, the production of oil and asphalt.
I feel keenly about this; I really do, because, rightly or wrongly, perhaps wrongly, I felt that in the speech I made in 1941, after having made a trip up to Fort McMurray and after having investigated the plant carefully, after having seen what they were doing there-and in my judgment they were doing a good job considering that they had every conceivable piece of pioneering work to do; I know the minister from Edmonton will bear me out that they had to discover everything-I had given a lead. It is quite true, as has been said before, that they had difficulties in discovering a method of taking the sand out of the pit. It was all pioneer work. There was nobody in America who knew how to do it better. But the Abasand company did overcome that, at the report submitted by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company stated. I have the report here and I shall read what they say about it. May I first deal with separation? This is the report of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company. They say:
We are of the opinion that the process of Abasand Oils Limited for separating the bitumen from the sands is a practical one which could be used in a large scale plant and which would yield reasonable results. Recoveries in the separation plant were consistently over ninety per cent.
They afterwards stated that the Chicago refining company, to w'hich the Consolidated

Mining and Smelting company engineers had sent quite a number of barrels, I believe, eighty barrels, reported that they got as high as ninety-seven per cent of oil. The Consolidated Mining and Smelting company were reliable. The minister sent them up there because they were reliable engineers. Their report to the minister stated that the refining was satisfactory. Then, Mr. Chairman, why in the name of heaven did the men not carry on? There have been so many different managers up there that I imagine each one will blame it on the other; the men who are there now I believe are called the General Engineering Company or some other name; I am not passing any comment on them. Apparently they are starting all over again. What did the others do who went ahead of them with it? I shall go back tq where I started. The minister tells us he had nothing to do with it. I am sorry he has not had anything to do with it. I am convinced that if he had anything to do with it, it would not be in the mess it is in to-day. I make that kind statement to the minister because he has done things.
I am beginning to think the hon. member is the man who got us into all this trouble.

That is why I am interested in it now. I like to go and see things. I like to devote my time and effort and the best I have toward developing this country. That is the joy I have out of life, to serve my country. Just as soon as I cannot render some service in this House of Commons to my native country I am going to retire from the House of Commons. There is. nothing in public life for me except service. What I do I do for the country. I try to do something for the country, and I repeat, I am glad that the minister is not responsible for the mess up there. I am sorry he did not have something to do with the matter. I am sure if he had had something to do with it, it would not be in the mess it is to-day.
The Consolidated Mining and Smelting company said that outside of the separation being satisfactory, the Abasand company had overcome the difficulties of mining. I know what the difficulties are; I was there. I was there several days on different occasions. I saw their planers operate. It was a good idea, but it did not work because when the planers come up against sand like that the sand wears the planers out. The Abasand people did not know that when they started to use planers instead of digging or picking the sand out the planers proved unsatisfactory. The Abasand

172i5
War Appropriation-Supplies
people did not think sand would wear the planers out, but they had to abandon them and then they went into blasting, which they found satisfactory. I saw that myself. I saw them blast many, many tons at a time. I saw how the sand disintegrated. I saw them use steam shovels and take it to the mill.
What was the trouble? What was the difficulty that the Abasand company had not overcome? Th%y had built a separation plant big enough to separate four hundred or more tons of sand a day. My 1942 picture shows the mill there and the refinery at the back of the mill. I have the picture of them here. The refinery was not big eiiough to take care of much more than half what the mill separated. If the Minister of Mines and Resources could have taken the time in 1943 to go up there before anything was done and could have talked to the Abasand men who were there and who had overcome many of the difficulties, and who were doing a good job, I do not believe he would have sent anybody up there but the. people who were there. I hold no brief for them. They are nothing to me. I am a stranger to them, but they were doing a good job. They had a new mill which they operated in 1942 when I was there. They turned out that summer from the 19th day of May to the 30th day of September, 17,000 barrels of oil. They could have turned out much more if the refinery plant had been of the same capacity as the separation plant. As I say, if the minister had had time to have gone there himself, I am satisfied that he would have done just as good a job there as he has done elsewhere, and we would now be producing oil up there in a big way, as it should be produced. Last fall when one of the engineers of the department, I believe it was Doctor Haanel, was before the committee, he told us of the necessity of producing oil; he explained that since 1930 the oil wells being tapped in the United States or blown in or coming into production had not been sufficient to keep up with the demand for oil, and how necessary it was that Canada should produce
oil.	Then, at page 923 of the proceedings of the committee for November 30, 1943, he went on to make this significant and more or less alarming statement as to what may be the ultimate outcome in connection with these oil sands:
I may say in passing there are various stories written about the anxiety which the United States is showing regarding their oil supplies. She lays great stress on the bituminous sands of Alberta but says that is a problem for us to take care of.
And so it is a problem for us Canadians. No one knows better than the minister how necessary it is for Canada to produce oil in a big way. I quite agree that under present conditions there may be limitations to what we can do. I was on the spot; I went up and down the river for some fifty or sixty miles. I know also that in their report to the minister the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company stated that by open-cut operations 50,000,000 barrels of oil could be taken out of that sand. That is something; it is much better than nothing. If the minister had just taken hold of this whole business right after he received the report of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company; if he had undertaken to carry on that business there, perhaps to-day a good part of those 50,000,000 barrels of oil would have been taken out.
Of course for the last thirty years engineers of the Department of Mines and Resources have been telling the world that we have the greatest and richest oil deposit in the world. Everyone knows how many wells you have to drill before you get one that will flow oil; I think only about one out of every ten is of real use. There at Fort McMurray, in the immediate area right around that little plant, according to the evidence submitted in these reports we have approximately 5,000,000 barrels. I believe that is the richest oil sand in the world, capable of producing one barrel of oil for each cubic yard of sand. Of course, as everyone knows, if you could get a well that would flow all the time that would be fine, but how do we get it? I do not want to say anything but the kindest about Turner valley, but look at the number of wells that have been drilled there. It has a production of perhaps
10,000,000 barrels a year, and that is not big oil. When I was last at Fort McMurray I met one of the most celebrated geologists in the world, a high official of the United States government. He said to me, "Mr. MacNicol, if you can get $10,000,000 out of the government at Ottawa I will get $10,000,000 at Washington and we could build a plant here, because this is the greatest deposit that I know of." That man goes all over the world for the United States government. Recently he was away down in South America; I had a letter from him, from Chile. I do not think he would make statements like this haphazardly, and it was a pity that in my speech in 1942 I could not persuade this government to put up $10,000,000 and the government at Washington to put up another $10,000,000, for maybe we would be producing perhaps 20,000 barrels of oil a day from these sands, and that is a good deal of oil to start with.
War Appropriation-Supplies

Now I want to show what the government has done. In this I am not finding fault with the minister; I think he made an honest attempt, but I should like to know how it got out of his hands. I am told now that the matter rests with the Department of Mines and Resources. The minister having started it, I now wish he had kept on with it; I am sure we would have had much better results than we have had so far. What did the minister hope for after he took over the plant? I quote from Hansard for April 14, 1943, at page 2153:
We hope to have a small commercial operation, as a by-product of the research this summer, producing bituminous material for the Alaska highway, so that there will be some revenue to offset the expenditure.
We all hoped there would be revenue from it. Now the Alaska highway has been built, and still we are not producing oil there. I do not know how far the minister can interfere with the Department of Mines and Resources, but I am sorry to say that the evidence given by officials of that department last fall before the reconstruction committee shocked me very much. It seemed to me that something was wrong. I always hoped, and so stated, that the mines and resources department would be completely in earnest in connection with the production of oil there, but just read the evidence given to the committee on November 30 last year. I do not like to refer to it; it did not show very much in the way of cooperation in connection with the production of oil at Fort McMurray. Did I understand the minister to say that the company operating the plant is a crown company?
No.
It belongs to the government?
No.
Then who owns it?

It is owned by the same
owners as before. We took over the plant in order to carry on certain explorations. I am not very familiar with the agreement, but I think the ownership remains as it was.

I have the agreement here, and I think it is worth quoting:
Whereas the oil controller, Department of Munitions and Supply, has recommended to the government that for the purpose of more effectively prosecuting the war

That was an extremely fine purpose.
-in which His Majesty is presently engaged, all possible sources of new oil supplies in Canada should be investigated and put into production if such is found feasible;
fMr. MacNicol.j
And whereas the government during the past thirty years has investigated the extent and quality of northern Alberta bituminous (or tar) sand deposits and the most conclusive result to date is that the Horse river reserve, near McMurray, is known to contain substantial deposits which because of their grade, location, and volume have the most immediate potential importance for petroleum production;
And whereas the contractor has carried on investigations since 1930 into machinery and processes for mining the Alberta tar sands, extracting the bitumen, and refining petroleum products therefrom. . . .
Then a little later on it states:
And whereas the oil controller, Department of Munitions and Supply, and the director of mines and geology branch. Department of Mines and Resources, recognizing the necessity of exploring all possibilities of producing petroleum products, greatly needed in this emergency and afterwards, have recommended that a test or pilot plant should be developed for the purpose of proving what can be produced from the Alberta bituminous or tar sands, and that an agreement should be entered into with the contractor under which its plant would be remodelled and enlarged, if necessary, to serve as such test or pilot plant to carry out the investigations referred to in the preceding paragraph, and also to produce needed asphalt and roadoils.
Then the government displaced the Abasand company management and sent in Mr. Smith, Mr. Irwin and others to operate the plant. If that is not a crown company why should the government make the first initial payment of $300,000. It is a crown company because the minister said that the crown was taking it over. Then a controller was appointed, and the evidence I have is that the controller either has not carried out his duties or has been displaced. Much is going on up there that he appears to know nothing about, and yet the agreement states emphatically that the controller must approve all plans and changes. I am sure that if the government accedes to the request of the provincial government of Alberta to appoint a royal commission it will be found that many changes have been made without the consent of the controller. I am told that evidence is available to prove that to be the case.
If this matter does not come under the minister's department, then he cannot answer and I shall have another opportunity to bring it up when the Minister of Mines and Resources comes before us. I want to know exactly what amount of money has been spent to date. According to these figures we have received little for the expenditures made. I am told that to-day there are approximately 150 employees. I am told also that there are three women there. What in the name of heaven are women doing in that part of the countrv, away in the backwoods? They must

War Appropriation-Supplies
be stenographers, but I do not think the Abasand company would require any women stenographers. When I was there the Abasand company had a staff of about seventy, but it is said there are 150 to-day falling over one another doing little, pulling down a building and sticking it up again somewhere else, going from post to pillar and hither to yon'.
According to the minister's statement about a million dollars has been spent. The Minister of Mines and Resources should be able to tell us just how much has been spent. When he does I will venture the Minister of Munitions and Supply will say, "Ob, if I had only had that money, what a job I could have done!" I am sure I could have done a much better job myself. I bet anything I would be producing oil to-day. I would gladly have given my time free of charge and' paid my own expenses to do so for the sake of this country, my land.
A few minutes ago the minister said that I am responsible for this. I feel somewhat responsible for having made a speech which seemingly conveyed to the Minister of Munitions and Supplies the idea that I was right. I feel pleased that he is convinced that there are great resources there, but I am sorry that there has been a waste of a million or more dollars, whatever it is, without a drop of oil or one pound of asphalt having been produced. Some one will have to give an account of where that money has gone. We shall have to have the name and address of each individual in that staff of 100 or 150 people. We want to know what they are doing. We want to know where all the lumber has gone that was brought in there, where all the tools are.
I am told that there is no one keeping track of the spades, wrenches and things of that sort being used. That is not the way to run a business. The minister would not run a business in that way, nor would I. When I was in business we had a tool department, and when any tool went out the man in charge kept a record. The man who took it out had to bring it back or pay for it. It is alleged that no one has kept track of the tools here. I know there has been considerable trouble in getting men, and I am told also that there are nearly as many bosses as there are men.
Max Ball in his day was usually on the job in Edmonton and there were three or four members of the executive at Fort McMurray when I was there. I want a full report of what was done with every dollar that went into this plant. I want to know how many times the different employees went back and forth between Edmonton and the plant. Why were people moved up there? What was the cost of moving their furniture
up there or bringing it out again. The country is entitled to know what was done with this million or a million and a half dollars. That is a lot of money when everyone is digging down into his pockets for the last dollar he can pinch in order to pay his income tax. That is a lot of money when every workman in our Canadian plants is having an income tax deduction made from his pay envelope. Some one will have to give an accotmt for this apparent waste of money. Some one will have to explain why there is no oil or asphalt to show for this expenditure. I support the request made by the Alberta government that a royal commission be appointed to go into this whole matter in order that we may know where we stand.

I realize that this discussion is quite irregular, because this matter comes under another department, but since my hon. friend has made a statement I should like to say a few words. I think he is mistaken about what we are trying to do at Abasand. We are trying to get information to see whether that deposit can be made into a large source of petroleum which can be sold at commercial prices. If it is a source of petroleum commercially obtainable it will warrant the expenditure of anywhere from $20 million to $50 million. If it is not a commercial source the government will not be warranted in spending any more money on the project. A small source of petroleum is of no value in that locality. The limited market there can be filled by the plant already there.
And which has been wiped out.

We could have stopped at any time and said, "No, it is not good enough; we are not warranted in exploring for further possibilities." We have made changes in the process from time to time, but that is the purpose of a plant of that kind, when being operated to get information. I sincerely hope that by June we shall know whether or not we have anything. In the meantime tests are going on in Chicago to see what process must be used to get rid of the high sulphur content. Other tests are being made by means of refinery runs to see what can be made of the product by using different processes.
As an engineer, I would say that all that is necessary before the government should be asked to commit itself for a huge sum of money. The money being spent to-day, largely for exploration work, is not too much, because we have been spending money, as
War Appropriation-Supplies

my hon. friend says, for the last thirty years. We should find out whether we are warranted in spending money to get production, or whether we are not warranted in Bpending money. If we are not, we should pull out. Within the next several months, I sincerely hope that we shall find out whether we are justified in going on. We are trying to exhaust every possibility. We have spent something less than S900,000 up to this moment.
Including the Consolidated?

Including everything. That amount of money is not excessive for explorations of that kind. We can go on spending two or three hundred thousand dollars a year, as we have for many years, and get nowhere, or we can spend a good deal of money and either arrive somewhere, or decide that there is no possibility of arriving anywhere. Therefore I suggest that my hon. friend do not look for immediate results in the way of profits. There are no profits coming out of the exploration that is going on to-day, but we hope to get information on which to base our future course.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was undoubtedly remiss in my duty a few moments ago. I did not want to stop the hon. member for Davenport from making his statement on the tar sands, but when the minister stated that the matter did not come within his department I should then have stopped the discussion, because we are always inclined in committee to have discussions that are repetitions. As the hon. member for Davenport said at the end of his remarks, there will be an opportunity for full discussion of this matter when the appropriate item in the estimates is reached, and I must therefore rule the discussion out of order.

I hesitate to discuss a matter that is entirely irrelevant to the estimates now under discussion, Mr. Chairman, but in fairness to the gentleman who is now general manager of Abasand Limited, I want to say that he is a prominent Toronto business man whose integrity and ability are not questioned. This gentleman, Mr. George B. Webster, has been in the office of the oil controller for some considerable time doing excellent work, and so far as I am concerned I think he will give a good account of himself not only with Abasand Limited, but in anything else which he undertakes to supervise.

Mr. Chairman, in the remarks I have to make on this question I wish to make it absolutely clear

that I have nothing to say reflecting on the honesty or integrity of anybody, though it may reflect on their business ability. But the main concern I have in this matter is that we should either get results or know the reason why. I was amazed at the remarks just made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I was under the impression that this matter was under his department, but when I got answers to questions I had put on the order paper the other day I noticed that they were brought down by the Minister of Mines and Resources. Nevertheless the Minister of Munitions and Supply has on every occasion dealt with this question of the development of the tar sands, and even to-day in making his presentation he dealt in part with the tar sands and said that he would make a further statement in regard to them in the near future. Last year it was the Minister of Munitions and Supply who was the only one to deal with this question on the government side of the house. I do not recall the Minister of Mines and Resources ever dealing with the tar sands. Certainly he has not done very much in that regard since the war started.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply said a moment ago that the main concern of his department in this matter was to get information. That is commendable. Information is essential.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am convinced that a discussion of the tar sands is absolutely out of order after the answer just given by the minister, who stated clearly that there will be ample opportunity to discuss this problem when the estimates of the Department of Mines and Resources are before the committee. I trust that the hon. member will respect the ruling of the Chair.

But the question has been under discussion, Mr. Chairman, and while it is up I should like to say a few words upon it. The minister was dealing with the question of getting information in regard to the Athabaska tar sands. That is probably one of the first essentials. But the minister should also understand that the Department of Mines and Resources,, through its research branch, has been working on this problem for over thirty years. Last year in the house, when the Minister of Munitions and Supply was speaking on this subject, he said that to his own knowledge they had been working on the tar sands for about thirty years, and the same evidence was given before the reconstruction committee last year.
