I believe that the
request is a reasonable one since the hon. member has assured the committee that there will be no repetition by members of his group; repetition has, of course, been criticized in the press several times, and I may also be criticized if I allowed them to go unnoticed.

Thank
you, Mr. Chairman. I shall take no longer than is necessary. I was discussing the part
which the Minister of Munitions and Supply had played in this matter every year, and it is surprising to me at least that the Minister of Munitions and Supply has been the only minister on the government benches who has seen fit to deal with this question. Some of the letters which I have in regard to the development of the tar sand, and particularly the experimental work that was carried on are letters written and signed by the Minister of Munitions and1 Supply, so that whether or not the matter comes directly under his department, it is certainly one in which he is directing the progress of development, and therefore he must share to a degree the responsibility for its progress.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: But he has just said he is not.

I have
letters here signed by the minister, written to the province of Alberta, and dealing with this question, so that he must have something to do with this development. It may be only the experimental work with which he is concerned. But certainly the letter which the Minister of Munitions and Supply wrote to the premier of Alberta on June 23, 1942, deals with this very problem. Let me read part of it:
War requirements for petroleum are so urgent, particularly in connection with the activities in northern Alberta, that the federal government wish to explore the possibilities for a large-scale development in the vicinity of the Abasand operation.
Tentative arrangements have been made to have the exploratory work carried out under the direction of officers of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. The deposits will be drilled to determine the quantities. The Abasand refinery runs will be checked and studied in an effort to determine refining costs. Laboratory tests, and possibly a full scale refinery run, will be carried out to determine whether the sulphur content can be dealt with in order that aviation gasoline can be obtained as one of the products.
This work is, of course, contingent on the approval and cooperation of your government. If the work is to be undertaken it is our desire that no more crown leases be granted in this area until a decision can be reached as to whether a large-scale development is warranted.
I would appreciate the favour of an early reply which will, I hope, offer the cooperation of your government in the studies which we propose to undertake.
This letter is signed by the minister. Therefore, definitely, he has something to do with it, because it was he who communicated with the government of Alberta to secure their cooperation, which they most readily agreed to give, as is evidenced in a letter which I have here dated July 3, 1942, in reply to the minister's letter, and signed by the then premier, the late Mr. Aberhart.
War Appropriation-Supplies

One of the things which astonishes me in the minister's letter is the statement:
It is our desire that no more crown leases be granted in this area until a decision can be reached as to whether a large-scale development
is warranted.
It is the only case of which I have recollection wherein any other enterprise has been asked to stay out of the development field. In almost every other field of prospecting for minerals, everybody has been encouraged to go in and assist the government in discovering and developing these natural resources. But here is one area, in the northern part of Alberta, which has the largest potential supply of gasoline in the world. It has been, estimated at 250 billion barrels, and our own government experts estimate it at over 100 billion barrels. Yet the dominion government request that nobody else be allowed to go in there and do anything in the line of development until this government has had a chance to see whether it is worth while or not.
That is a peculiar attitude to take. I have studied the report of the reconstruction and reestablishment committee with regard to this development of the Abasand tars by the Abasand oil company, and the vagueness of the evidence is amazing. The issue is continually evaded. In almost every instance there is contradiction. One cannot but get the impression of a design to stall the operations and development of that Abasand company.
I believe such an attitude would be unwarranted even in peace time. How clearly it is exemplified I shall endeavour to point out in greater detail as we go on.
Let us look at the research plant here at Ottawa which is concerned with this matter. The Department of Munitions and Supply has something to do with it; there is no getting away from that. It is clearly indicated by letters which I have here.
May I interpose at this point that I think the Minister of Munitions and Supply has done a wonderful job as far as developing our war effort is concerned. I have said so before. But this is one place, or I should say, this is one more place where the government has definitely fallen down on its responsibility. I should like to see the whole thing put under the Department of Munitions and Supply, because I think the minister is capable, and I was agreeably surprised to learn to-day that he has not anything actively to do with it.
This plant in Ottawa has spent, in one instance that I know of, in the development of tar sands, over 8500,000. It is recorded in Hansard in a statement of the Minister of Munitions and Supply last year that the plant has been engaged for thirty years on research

in the development of tar sands. But we are not even yet at the place where we know where they are1 going. Let us turn to some of the evidence in this regard. On page 921 of the evidence given before the reconstruction committee, Mr. W. B. Timm', director of the mines and geology branch, Department of Mines and Resources, says:
While the results of this research work- That is, research carried on here at Ottawa.
will be of real value to any research work carried out in a larger plant, they wall not serve to guide engineers in the design of a commercial plant.
Well, now what in the world have we been doing for the last four years, ever since the war started? According to the minister's own words this is an urgent matter. He appealed to the province of Alberta for cooperation. Its urgency was stressed on the ground that we were short of gasoline. If that is so, this report is not very encouraging.
Let me cite some more evidence. On page 923 Mr. Timm says:
We therefore recommend that the unit best adapted for our investigations should be of the dimensions that can be termed semi-technical.
For thirty years they have been doing research work on this problem. The war has now lasted for over four years. Gasoline is one of our most precious and vital supplies. We have spent about a million dollars on development work. Now they say they want a larger unit because "the unit best adapted for our investigations would be one that can be termed semi-technical." The plant they have now is not, they say, suitable for their investigations.
The functions of the proposed new laboratory and plant are to investigate various processes involving hydrogenation applied to Canadian raw materials such as coals, bitumen, heavy crude oils, and residuums from petroleum refining that can be utilized as sources of gasoline or other liquid fuels.
It is amazing that after thirty years of research, after spending around a million dollars, they have finally decided that the plant which they have been using for experimental purposes is of no use whatever for the design of a commercial plant, and now they want a larger one.
May I quote a little further from this evidence, on page 922:
As stated previously, a small experimental hydrogenation plant for studying the manufacture of synthetic liquid fuels from such sources as coal, bitumen, et cetera, has been established.
That is the one here in Ottawa on Booth street.
This is as far as Canada has gone to provide substitute fuels for such a contingency.

War Appropriation-Supplies
So that the evidence given before that committee is that that is as far as they have gone, though over a million dollars has been expended on this development, in research.
This effort while of considerable value in providing scientific information can in no sense be considered as a major contributing factor to the solution of the problem under discussion.
Here in the statements which I have read is the evidence that the progress made to date is anything but satisfactory and they do not even know yet what the prospects are for these Abasand deposits. Let us see more of the evidence. Asked the question, before the committee:
What success have you had?
They state:
We believe the results are encouraging but v'e cannot go nearly far enough with the small help we have.
The further question was asked:
What would you require in the way of an enlarged plant to make your researches more effective?
The answer was:
That is really the plan now that is being presented here.
Up to date they have not had facilities to make their researches effective and what efforts they have been making have consisted in playing around with the subject. Is there any wonder then that the provincial government of Alberta has come to the point where it says that it looks as if there had been a deliberate effort to sabotage these tar sands?
The plant at Fort McMurray has been referred to, and the progress there has been apparently anything but satisfactory. In this evidence, at page 930, they make a further statement with reference to the plant in the north. Let me read one question:
Q.	You spoke about having a plant in mind there with a volume of 200 gallons a day?
A. That is what we would like to have.
Q. Presuming the funds were available, how long do you think it would take to erect that plant and equip it with the necessary machinery?
A. That is very hard to say under present conditions.
Q. But you could give us an estimate?
A. A very rough guess would be a year and a half.
The minister said that they would have sufficient knowledge to know whether they would go on with it around June. Here the request of this geological research committee is for a new plant to go ahead with an order to obtain further knowledge in regard to these sands. They want sufficient money to build the new plant and they figure it will take about a year or a year and a half. That does not coincide with what the minister said a
moment ago. There is a discrepancy between these statements, and I submit that a thorough investigation should be made to ascertain what progress is being achieved there. I am sure that the Minister of Munitions and Supply would be one of the first men to put his hand to that task and to say, "We will go ahead with this thing properly," because I have enough confidence in him to know that this would be the stand he would take.
Now may I read, with reference to this plant, something that was said in the Alberta legislature the other day. In the provincial legislature in Edmonton this question was being discussed and the provincial minister of public works, the Hon. Mr. Fallow, made reference to it. This is what he said in regard to the construction of that plant in Athabaska. I take it, as stated by the hon. member who spoke before me, that the provincial minister of public works, holding the position he does, must have a sense of responsibility. He has visited the plant on several occasions; he is minister of public works of Alberta; it is to their credit to see that the work is carried on, and if it is not being properly carried on to the extent that the provincial government thinks it should go, it is to their interest to proceed on their own and to carry out some development in this regard. I make these observations to indicate that the minister of public works of Alberta must have a sense of responsibility, and when he comments upon that development of the Athabaska tar sands, he must have something serious in mind. Well, this is what he said:
The $500,000 which had been appropriated by the dominion government to investigate the possibilities of large-scale production from the oil sands had all been spent in building modern dwellings, dormitories and workshops, sufficient to accommodate a much greater number of people than the plant required. This modern town was equipped with an up-to-date waterworks and sewage system; a modern electric light plant, buildings steam heated, a modern sawmill installed which cut the 400,000 feet of lumber used in the buildings, and not a dollar spent on the construction of a separation plant or to instal a piece of refinery equipment, and we were told that operations were going to be closed down because the money had all been spent.
That bears out the statement which was made by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), who personally visited the ground. If we take the two statements together-and these gentlemen have probably never seen each other-there must be some truth in what has been said when they make the same assertions. Here is' a town employing approximately 155 people, according to the return that was given me; yet it is modem
War Appropriation-Supplies

in almost every sense, with waterworks, electric lights and everything else, $500,000 having been already spent on modern buildings, and yet not one dollar has been spent on refinery equipment or a separation plant. If that is not a colossal waste of public money, and, I would also say, a deliberate attempt at sabotaging that development for years to come, I should like to know what to call it.
The speech goes on:
The stories I got from men who were working on the project made me wonder if the dominion government had borrowed some of the inmates of an insane asylum to handle the work. Some of the men who left the job told me they could stand it no longer. They thought everybody was crazy. They told me that trenches were dug and forms were put in to run the concrete foundations and the next day a gang of men would start digging other trenches close by and throw the earth into the hole they had dug the day before. Buildings were started and then torn down or moved to temporary foundations and finally they started putting the buildings on skids instead of foundations so that they could move them around with tractors to suit everybody's convenience. Trenches were dug for sewer and waterlines and the waterlines laid and backfilled without testing pipes for leaks. Later, when the water was turned on, the lines leaked so badly that the trenches had to be reopened and the lines taken up.
Then he states that this was done in the winter when the ground was frozen. The evidence is quite clear that there was a colossal waste of public money and it does warrant investigation.
Later on he says:
I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that on the two occasions when I visited this plant there was certainly no evidence of a shortage of manpower or machinery.
Apparently, therefore, that excuse could not be given, that there was a shortage of manpower, or machinery, which was the excuse given in the return brought down to me.
There was enough machinery and man-power to handle half a dozen plants of this size, most of which was idle.
I am quoting all this so that the committee will see that there must be some grounds for the statement in regard to the laxity of the dominion government in developing these sands.
Farther on in his speech he had this to say:
No construction work was done that it was not changed at least once. Changes three to five times were not uncommon. It will perhaps be conservative to say twenty-five per cent of the workmen were continuously engaged in tearing down some of what the other seventy-five per cent had put up.
This condition continued until the end of January and at that time no -work whatever, either on the separation plant or refinery had been done since the General Engineering Company took over. During the last few daj's of

January some men were started on the boiler-room building, but at the end of this month no more than one per cent of the work had been done there-this in spite of the following facts. . . .
Then he goes on and reports a lot of facts.
I received a return to a motion of mine in which I asked the following questions:
Has the pilot plant been started yet? If so, how long before it will be completed?
The answer to the first part of the question is: "Yes." The pilot plant has been started; but according to the speech which Mr. Fallow made in the legislature just a boiler-room had been started and very little work was done on that. The answer given here is correct although it may be misleading. Then the following answer is given to the second part of the question dealing with the time in which the plant will be completed:
. . . date of completion depends on delivery of equipment and materials, and availability of labour.
According to the minister of public works of Alberta who visited that plant on two different occasions, there was no shortage of manpower and there was no shortage of equipment, because the Abasand company at least had been producing-I am. now speaking from memory.-about four hundred barrels of crude oil a day. Surely we can do as good as that. The amazing thing is that although we spent thirty years in investigating these tar sands, yet to-day we have no information, that would lead to the construction of a large commercial plant. We find to-day these things are continually being deferred as time goes on, The evidence produced indicates clearly to me that something drastic should be done in this connection.
In the course of my remarks I said that on one occasion the research department had spent $500,000. I should like to read a little of the evidence to show what a disgraceful performance the whole thing has been. Mr. Ells appeared as a witness before the reconstruction and reestablishment committee. Mr. Ells is the engineer in the fuels division of the Department of Mines and Resources. He was asked this question:
Is it not true that some years ago two carloads of these tar sands were sent over to England for experimental purposes?
I wish to read what he said to show how evasive his evidence was. Some investigation should be made into this matter. On page 964 of the evidence contained in the minutes of proceedings and evidence No. 33, the hon. member for Davenport asked the following question:
May I ask Doctor Ells one further question; Doctor, I said this morning that I had read sometime prior to 1936 or 1935 that a con-

War Appropriation-Supplies
siderable quantity of tar sands had been sent to England for testing under the Freeman process of extraction of oil from the sand; have you ever heard of that; or, have you any recollection in regard to that having been done?
Doctor Ells: 1 have heard of it but I think the results have not been given out.
He does not know for sure. He says: "I have heard of it." That is a vague recollection. Mind you, two carloads of Athabaska tar sands were sent clear to England at an expense of $500,000, and Mr. Ells, who was giving evidence said:
I have heard of it but I think the results have not been given out.
He was then further questioned about this matter and on the next page he says:
No, I have not any definite recollection.
That is, he has no definite recollection of its having been sent to England. I think I should go back to the next page and read the question of the hon. member for Davenport, which was as follows:
Have you any recollection of the sand having been sent to England?
The answer is:
No, I have not any definite recollection.
If anybody sent two carloads of Athabaska tar sands over to England at an expense of- with the investigation which was carried out- $500,000, there is something wrong with his memory if he does not even remember it. His answer goes on:
I do recall that some years before that there were two carloads went over to England, to Cardiff, Wales, and a rather large amount of money spent in testing a method-I think about $500,000.
Mr. MacNicol: It was sent over to Cardiff?
Doctor Ells:	Yes, two carloads; I shipped
them myself.
Mr. MacNicol: What was the process used?
Doctor Ells: It was a secret process; it was so secret that the work was all done under the surveillance of the metropolitan police and nobody was allowed near the plant. They did not give anything out. The two men working on it, as I recall, died, and nothing was given out.
Just a few moments before that he said he did not remember the tar-sand being sent to England. There is something fishy about this, Mr. Chairman. You cannot tell me that that would not be a vivid recollection in one's mind. If that is the kind of men we have developing or carrying on the investigation work in Athabaska tar sands, heaven help us if we have to depend upon them for our war supplies. I am not trying to insinuate that Mr. Ells is not a reliable man, because I have read some of the articles he has written on the tar sands and they are excellent and give a glowing picture of the prospects in that
area. But why does he come before a committee, such as the reconstruction and reestablishment committee, and throw cold water on the whole thing? There is something sinister behind it.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply wrote to the government of Alberta and said that it is an urgent matter. We are told it is a necessity. We even have to ration gasoline to the people. I could say something about that, which I shall do some day. I have spoken on that question before in the house. I have some personal knowledge in that regard, but I do not intend to bring it up just now. Is it any wonder that the provincial government passed a resolution the other day in the Alberta legislature? I shall read the resolution. On page 4 of No. 22 votes and proceedings of the legislative assembly of the province of Alberta, the following appears:
Whereas, on June 23, 1912, the dominion government advised the Alberta government that "war requirements for petroleum are so urgent that the dominion government wish to explore the possibilities for a large-scale development in the vicinity of the Abasand operation," and requested the cooperation of the Alberta government in withholding the granting of any more crown leases until a decision can be reached as to whether a large-scale development is warranted; and
Whereas, large sums of money have been appropriated . . .
On a point of order, is it permissible to read the proceedings of a provincial legislature in this committee?
Yes.
I think so.
It is merely a statement of something that is already passed. It is in the press, Mr. Chairman, and is public information.
If it is not derogatory to the activities of the House of Commons I believe it may be read.

I shall
continue:
Whereas, large sums of money have been appropriated by the dominion government and spent on the construction of fully modern dwellings, dormitories, workshops, construction machinery, etc., far in excess of reasonable requirements, but no plant has yet been erected and no actual steps have been taken to demonstrate the possibilities for a large-scale development of the Athabaska oil sands.
Mr. Chairman, I say that this is definitely derogatory to this House of Commons, and I ask for your ruling.

Where is the point of order?
War Appropriation-Supplies
The hon. member is reading a statement made in the provincial legislature which I think is derogatory to this House of Commons.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: While I believe it is not in order to read from a previous debate in the House of Commons during the present session, after all the document being quoted by the hon. member is a public document dealing with what took place in a provincial legislature, and I think it may be quoted.
I understand that it becomes a public document when I read it, and I am quite prepared to ;able it when I am through.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The point the minister was making is that any document which is derogatory or which attempts to attack anything done by a department of government should not be read in the House of Commons. It was on that point that the minister rose, and I do not think a statement to that effect should be read in this chamber.
Mr. GRA\ DON: On the point of order, I think the minister and his parliamentary assistant are confusing a reflection on parliament with a reflection on the government, and the two are entirely different. My understanding of the remarks of the hon. member is that this resolution has already appeared in a large section of the press of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The hon. member is
reading from a statement made in the Alberta legislature.

Surely if the press of
Canada have a right to report it, there is nothing to hinder anyone from reading it in this House of Commons. I think we are carrying this matter of "not in the public interest" a little far if we stretch it to cover this point. As far as this party is concerned, Mr, Chairman, I am going to ask you to rule in favour of the hon. member who has been reading the document, because I do not see a question of privilege there.

This resolution is published in the votes and proceedings of a provincial legislature. It is a resolution of the legislature, which expresses the point of view of a provincial government. If it is critical of the federal government that is not to say it is critical of or derogatory to this parliament as a whole.
It might even reflect the views of a majority in this house.

That is conceivable,
given time, but I am not going to discuss that. Surely a resolution passed in a provincial 
legislature, dealing with intergovernmental matters, may be read in this house, particularly since it is part of the public records of that province, which has appeared in the press and is included in the votes and proceedings of that legislature. I think the minister and his parliamentary assistant are taking a wrong view of this.

Then I would be very much interested if my hon. friend could carry on and explain to me what item of the estimates is now being discussed. The entire evening has been spent in discussing a matter which does not come in any way under the Department of Munitions and Supply, and which does not involve one dollar appropriated to this department. I suggest that you have given sufficient latitude, Mr. Chairman, and I should like a ruling on that point.
That is an entirely different question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In setting forth the
position of the Chair earlier in the evening I stated that probably I was at fault in this matter when I allowed the hon. member for Davenport to go on with his speech, in view of the objection taken by the Minister of Munitions and Supply that the matter came under the Department of Mines and Resources. Later, however, when I attempted to express a ruling on the point, I believe unanimous consent was given to the hon. member for Bow River to continue with his remarks. I have already given my ruling on the point of order raised in connection with the reading of a resolution passed by the Alberta legislature. I believe it is in order as long as no reflection is cast upon the procedure or activities of the House of Commons.

Before the
hon. member goes on I think we should get one point of procedure straight. Several times a question has been raised as to whether or not the hon. member was in order in continuing this discussion. May I point out that we are discussing the war appropriation resolution, which relates to the defence of this country and to national security. The estimates now before the committee are presented in this way purely by arrangement and for the convenience of the committee. As far as the rules of this house are concerned there is nothing to prevent any hon. member from conducting a discussion on the army, or on naval affairs, or on the air force; no one can stop him. These items are before us in this way purely for our convenience. I am quite in agreement that we should keep to the arrangement we have made; otherwise the

War Appropriation-Supplies
discussion would wander all over the place. However, no one can rule the hon. member out of order for discussing anything relating to the prosecution of the war or the welfare of the country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are dealing with the war appropriation resolution which, as the hon. member has stated, would permit a very wide discussion to be carried on. The Minister of Munitions and Supply, however, has stated to the committee definitely that the matter of the Alberta tar sands under discussion this evening does not come under his department, so that I suggest that we should allow the hon. member for Bow River to go on and that will be the end of that discussion. Many times we are accused by hon. members, and even in the press, of having a great deal of repetition in this chamber. I am sure hon. members can readily see that when the estimates of the Department of Mines and Resources are before the committee we are likely to have repeated what we have heard so far this evening. That is the position as I see it.

I should like to point out that apparently we have wasted about thirty years, as far as this matter is concerned, under the Department of Mines and Resources. It is about time that jurisdiction was given to another department, preferably Munitions and Supply, so that we may make some headway. Would that be in order?

The resolution continues:
Whereas, this apparent waste of public funds and the lamentable loss of valuable time in tearing down the Abasand plant, constructing dwellings, dormitories and workshops and in other activities which are only incidental to the demonstration of an economic process for the commercial extraction of oil products has created grave fears and misgivings in the minds of the public that the whole development of the Athabaska oil sands is being systematically sabotaged; now, therefore,
Be it resolved, that this legislature petition the dominion government to set up immediately a royal commission of inquiry, with specific instructions to investigate all activities on and in connection with the Abasand oil properties since June 23, 1942, to ascertain why, despite the large sums of public funds which have been spent, no plant has been erected or equipment installed and no actual experimental work carried on to determine the possibilities of extracting oil products in commercial quantities from the Athabaska oil sands.
It might be of interest to note further that when the vote was taken on this resolution all the Liberals and Conservatives, who in Alberta are known as independents, voted against any inquiry to find out why this situation existed in Athabaska. They were solidly of the opinion
that the laxity, indifference and jeopardy to our war effort should continue. The votes and proceeedings records their names, as follows:
Messieurs MacLaclilan, Bowlen, Mahaffy, Walker, Martin, Macdonald. Jackson, O'Brien (Dr.), Campbell (Dr.), Tellier, Brown, Laut, Broomfield, McKinnon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has spoken for forty minutes.
Since I have been interrupted so often-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have allowed six minutes for interruptions.

As the member for Athabaska I desire to voice a most strenuous protest against the proceedings to-night. I have not been in a position to take part in this debate because my documents were not available. This debate has been allowed to proceed entirely out of order and I protest as strongly and strenuously as I can.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is rather a reflection upon the Chair. I do not know whether the hon. member was in the committee when I made the ruling, but I took the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the committee into my confidence before I gave the ruling. When the minister made his presentation this afternoon, tar sands were mentioned, so that it was rather hard for the Chair to rule against this debate, and the minister felt the same way on that subject.
In my judgment you are entirely in order.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to carry on the discussion on tar sands. In his lengthy address this afternoon the minister made reference to various forms of fuel which are made use of in carrying out our war effort. He referred to coal, wood, gas and oil, and I wish to ask him to be good enough to inform the committee as to what developments have taken place in connection with the processing of coal at the mine. Experiments have been going on in this country, and it is quite evident that considerable benefit would be derived from a more economical use of the coal we have. I am given to understand that in the United Kingdom about one-sixth of the coal mined is put through a process immediately which produces not only fuel but various by-products. Before the war a great deal of work was done in Germany, both in an experimental and in a commercial way, with regard to brown coal. It is the belief of many to-day that the German scientists have solved the question that baffled scientists in past years and are
War Appropriation-Supplies

able to produce lubricating as well as fuel oil. We believe that in Russia the coal mined at several fields is processed at the mine to produce a gas which can be carried to other parts of the country.
Canada is a country of great spaces; our coal is mined at places far distant from the centres of population, and for purposes of economy it may become necessary to produce the fuel and the by-products at the mine. What we do now is to mine the coal and spend tens of thousands of dollars in carrying it elsewhere where it is burned most wastefully. It is computed that something like two-thirds of its intrinsic value goes up the chimney to the detriment of our health and property. If we could produce fuel and by-products at the mine we could provide employment for men and could make a more economical use of this natural resource. This would prove of great benefit to the transportation companies which would carry goods to the communities in the mining areas and then carry out the products of the mines. I have no doubt that in considering fuel matters the minister has given due thought to the experiments which have been going on, and I should like him to give us the benefit of his opinion as to the prospect of using coal in this more economical fashion.
I phould like time to examine the statements and obtain the opinions of my experts. I shall try to make a statement on this matter before the debate ends.

I
should like to ask a few questions, but first I wish to offer a suggestion to the Minister of Munitions and Supply. He has under his control many plants employing thousands of workers. A few weeks ago most of these workers were handed income tax forms to be returned by April 30. The majority of these workers are very much troubled at the present time. While these income tax forms are supposed to be easy to make out, the fact is that they are extremely difficult. I understand that in each of these plants there is a munitions and supply office, and I suggest to the minister that he arrange to have one, two or three people placed at the service of the workers to assist in making out their income tax forms. I would suggest also that the Minister of Munitions and Supply take up with the Minister of National Revenue, who unfortunately is not present this evening, to see if these workers-many of these plants are many miles from an income tax office- cannot be permitted to pay their income taxes at offices in the plants in which they
IMr. Stirling.]
work. In many instances these workers thought all their income tax had been deducted for 1943 and they are now finding that they have paid only half the tax. I feel, and I imagine the minister may feel the same way, that it would assist in keeping up the morale in these plants if this suggestion were carried out.
During the last year something else has cropped up which has not helped the morale of our workers. When many of these men go home at nights they are unable to have the benefit of their radios, because at the present time it is almost impossible to buy new radio tubes. One of the many controls exercised by the minister is in connection with the manufacture of radio tubes and his department issues releases to these manufacturers. I suggest that he see to it that proper materials are released so that tubes may be manufactured and these workers again given the benefit of their radios. This matter may rightly belong to another department, but I have talked to the minister and I know he is anxious to have these workers in the best of spirits. I think this would help considerably.
I have a few questions to ask on the first item. I should like to know just what plants have stopped work, where they are situated, and what munitions they were making. When a contract is given for the making of a boat or something of that kind, are wages allowed to be bulked instead of details being given to the minister's department? I should also like to know what large machines are rented by the minister's department for his different plants, such as travelling cranes and large machines for handling work in the plant.
There have been complaints that machine tools have been left idle in plants for many months and the workers, of course, feel that these machine tools should be working on something. I appreciate the fact that the munitions or guns these machine tools were turning out have perhaps reached their production peak for the present, but I was wondering whether there was not something that these id-le machines could be put to work on.
The minister mentioned this afternoon that sales were being made to the United States. Would he tell us just what the United States are buying from us at the present time and have been during the past year, and to what amount? Could the minister also tell us if there is any chance of the Nobel plant being opened again, and just why was that plant closed?
There is another matter I will mention now since the minister in his speech mentioned wartime housing and staff houses. I bring the

War Appropriation-Supplies
question up now because in Peterborough, Ontario, in the riding I represent, I know one staff house which has so few persons in it that I feel it could be put to better use if it- were turned into a hospital for the army, the navy or the air force, or for them all, instead of being left as a staff house. It is well equipped, has large dining-rooms, good bathrooms and every facility, and with very little trouble ramps could be made to take the place of the few steps leading up to the different floors, in order that the chairs and beds could be moved from floor to floor easily. Will the minister answer now or later?

I shall attempt to answer
now. So far as income tax goes, I have to have the help of the Minister of National Revenue to make out mine, so that I am afraid I would not be of much help to the man in Peterborough in making out his income tax return. But I will call the attention of my colleague the Minister of National Revenue to the remarks of my hon. friend.

Perhaps you
help the Minister of National Revenue to make his out? '

But
does not the minister think it is a good idea?

I think it would be a great
idea-wonderful.

It is past a laughing matter with the worker. I know that some of these workers are simply at their wits' end as toi what they can do. On top of that, they have to go to the post office and get a money order to send their money in. They are put to great expense in order to look after something I really believe the government should do. In order to carry on his department the Minister of Munitions and Supply must -have the income tax from these workers; that is where the minister comes in; he needs the money to carry on his department, and I feel that he should do everything possible for these workers.

I am not disagreeing with my hon. friend in the least. I think every man should have expert advice in making out his income tax. No one needs it more than I do, and no one direads the job more than I do, so that I feel for the workers. I will take the matter up with the Minister of National Revenue.
As to radio tubes, the difficulty is not materials but manufacturing capacity. There is nothing more urgently required for war purposes than radio tubes, and there is no field in which we have made a greater attempt
to expand capacity. We have made a certain number of radio tubes that have gone to the retail trade. They have not been too well distributed, and we are checking on that. To-day we are making about what we used to make in pre-war years, and we feel that we are going a long way in invading war capacity in doing that. It has been suggested recently that we should have distribution of radio tubes under control, and we may make them a controlled item shortly. That is usually effective in straightening out distribution troubles. I assure my hon. friend that we are doing the best we can on that item.
There is a definite black market in radio tubes, and if there were some check on distribution it might help a great deal.

I am not sure about the black market, but I do know that distribution is not very satisfactory. It is a tight supply and demand situation.
As to plants that have been closed, I cannot give my hon. friend offhand the plants that have been closed. The only one I can think of at the moment is Nobel, and the reason was that the demand for explosives from Canada dropped sharply. Part of our capacity was stand-by capacity, built at a time when British plants were being bombed very heavily. Later there was a demand for that capacity from the United States. But when the plants in the United States came into production the demand dropped. In order to carry out our production here in three plants with some degree of economy it was necessary to close one, and there were certain reasons why the Nobel plant seemed to be the obvious one to close. My hon. friend asked if there is a chance that it will be needed again. Certainly there is a chance. To-day bombs are dropping in Britain, and if a bomb dropped on a large explosive plant there, Britain would no doubt require extra production from Canada. For that reason it is very difficult to dismantle any plant. We are never sure that it will not be needed again. Part of our capacity was built as stand-by capacity, and we must use it as such until the war ends.
Are we importing at the present time any explosives of the type we made at Nobel?
No.
Not propellents?

We did for a short time. We had a T.N.T. line that was being run at a very small capacity; we wanted to convert

War Appropriation-Supplies
that line to something else, and for a time we did import a small amount of T.N.T. It was a dropping requirement. We did it to tide us over a temporary situation.
Have all the men who were employed at Nobel been given other employment?
Yes.
Has no dismantling been done at Nobel?
We took out a small chemical unit, moved it to Calgary and installed it there. If we again need full capacity at Nobel we could easily move it back. It is one of three duplicate units
The premises are now in the hands of caretakers?

Yes.
Did I finish answering the questions of the hon. member for Peterborough West? He said something about the staff house, I believe.
Yes.

That staff house is not operating with occupancy sufficient to warrant keeping it open, and we have offered it to the Department of Pensions and National Health. I know the officers of that department have examined it. I am not just sure what the report was. In any event I quite agree with my hon. friend that under the circumstances we should not keep it open.

I
might add that these staff houses are built in such a way that during the winter months, and especially in the spring, they have to be heated; otherwise the plywood which is inside would warp and the buildings would deteriorate in no time. All of them will have to be kept heated.
Yes.

I should like to ask the minister a question, following the question which was asked him last night, with respect to the air training schools which are likely to fall victims to the decision that many of them have to be closed. The minister, replying to a question last evening, said that these schools would not be allowed to depreciate. Perhaps that is not the answer which we were looking for.	'
I said that the runways would not be allowed to deteriorate.

The minister could put a few watchmen on there and perhaps that would do the trick. But what I would ask the minister -is this. As the basis of my

question, may I remind him that when these air training schools were built and manned by the staff, and were operating, where they were built in small communities, perhaps adjacent to a town or village, the population of those communities increased to the extent in some cases of being nearly doubled. I understand that the government has now in mind putting something else into these schools, so that instead of being run by air personnel they will be applied to some other use. The complaint which begins to come to us is this. Many people have invested money, perhaps in small businesses, perhaps in remodelling their homes, because these air schools have acute housing difficulties; sometimes town councils have asked the residents to do all they could to accommodate the additional people coming in. After having run for, perhaps, not more than three years, some of these schools are to be closed, and the local town is simply going back to the position it was in before the war. In some cases people will lose money on their investments. I realize, of course, that if the war were to end to-morrow, that would be the end of the schools, and the inevitable will come, but some of us. have received a good many communications from these communities-from individuals, from boards of trade and other organizations

with respect to this matter. Would the minister amplify his answer of last evening and tell us if the government has any plan whereby the schools can be operated in some other way, so that these communities will not be set back commercially, financially and otherwise.

The disposal of the fields will be handled in this way. In due course they will be declared surplus to Royal Canadian Air Force requirements. I may say that up to this time none has been so declared. When they are, they will pass to the war assets disposal committee. The committee will inquire of all government departments whether any department has use for any portion of the assets of that field. The Department of Transport will take over the field itself and such buildings as it believes to be useful for an airport to meet civil aviation requirements. The other buildings, as I have said, will be offered to other departments. If there are no claimants they will pass to the War Assets Corporation, which will dispose of them in a manner which will bring .about the greatest good to the greatest number; a decision that will require very careful study.
That, I understand, is the procedure. I think that people in the towns concerned must have realized that the school was there for a longer or shorter period depending upon the requirements of the air training programme. It

War Appropriation-Supplies
would have been hardly reasonable to suppose that so tremendous a programme would go on indefinitely. Naturally, pilots have to be trained before they can be used, and logically the training would not continue to the end of the war. There comes a time when all reasonable requirements for number of pilots have been met. That is about the best answer I can give my hon. friend.

Is the minister now in a position to answer the several questions I asked him, in particular with regard to the plan for the liquidation of war-time industry or its translation into civilian production? What is the plan the minister has in mind in that regard? Several months ago, I think it was last November, an article appeared in the press to the effect that the government had decided to free as far as possible, within the limitations of the safety of the state, many unnecessary economic controls which had prevailed since the outbreak of war. Demobilization of a war industry to change from wartime into civilian industry, to the end that civilian wants may be satisfied without detriment to the war effort, and also the liquid? -tion of unnecessary war-time controls, are matters within the knowledge of the minister and in respect of which I asked certain questions this evening.

My hon. friend has given me a good deal of territory to cover. He seems to press me for plans. He pressed me very hard for the government's plan for ' civil aviation. I gave it to him last Friday, and apparently he does not know what to do with it now he has it. I believe that if he will think back he will realize that, since this parliament opened, we have given out our plans to a considerable extent. I think that in the matter of planning for post-war development we have announced our plans step by step in advance of any other country. My hon. friend referred to the Baruch report on the disposal of surplus war assets. I might point out that our plan of disposal was announced some months before that plan came out. As far as disposal goes, we are almost exactly parallel with the proposals of the Baruch report. I would point out, however, that our plan is in operation, while the other at the moment is only a plan although the personnel has been appointed in the last two or three weeks.
Will the minister explain the plan that is in operation? That is what we want to know. What is the plan?

The plan has been explained. There will be legislation covering it. At the moment it is in operation under the War
Measures Act and it was set up before parliament met. We are getting all the experience we can to enable us to bring in the best bill possible, and before parliament rises there will be a bill to cover the disposal situation.
The procedure is this. There are two bodies. One is the Crown Assets Disposal Committee. That committee is made up of representatives of all war services and two or three departs ments outside that which have special interest in disposal problems, and it also includes a representative of labour, a representative of the farming industry and a representative of householders. Any item that is declared surplus to government requirements first goes before the committee. It is really a policy committee, or at least it is a committee to advise the minister and the government on policy in connection with various items. If an item declared surplus by one department can be useful to another department, that fact is noted in the report to the minister. In any event, the committee recommends a procedure. If it recommends that the item should be disposed of, it is so reported to the government, and the government by order in council turns the item over to the War Assets Corporation for disposal. The policy of disposal as advised by the committee is passed on to the War Assets Corporation as an instruction. The War Assets Corporation then studies the disposal of the item in the best interests of the greatest number of people. If it is an item of common purchase it will be put into retail channels in such a way that every part of the country will have a fair opportunity of purchasing the article.
I might point out that at this stage the items being dealt with by the corporation are not items of that class. They are usually surplus materials left from the cancellation of a contract, or they may be obsolete aeroplanes or an overage battleship. The disposal is studied by experts who make up the board of directors of the War Assets Corporation, and the War Assets Corporation may find that it is possible to dispose of the article in one of a number of ways. The company advises the government of the price that can be obtained, and the recommendation is either accepted by the government and the sale made, or it is rejected and the corporation is asked to find some other means of disposal.
That, I think, is a brief outline of the work of the committee and the company. It has taken some time to put the various items through the procedure. Great care is taken, both by the committee and by the corporation, in working out its procedure. In fact, no sale has finally been completed by the corporation at this date. It will be the policy of the corporation to make frequent reports. Parliament
War Appropriation-Supplies

will be kept well advised, and I can assure my hon. friend, that it is the purpose of this plan to work inside the goldfish bowl, as recommended by the Baruch report.
Mr. Chairman-
Does my hon. friend mind if I finish with this list of questions first?
How do you advertise that you have something for sale?

I do not advertise that I have anything for sale. It is the work of the corporation, and the corporation has sold nothing yet. Therefore let us leave the corporation to work until it has actually made some sales and we shall then report to the house.
I am answering now the question asked by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). About the plan for the demobilization of economic controls, which is rather an elaborate way of saying, how do you get rid of controls once you have them, if my hon. friend notices the control orders advertised from week to week he will find that we are dropping them every week. The purpose of the control is to take charge of an article in short supply and increase supply to meet needs, or, failing that, to distribute the article to meet war needs as the first priority and civilian needs after war needs have been filled. That is the purpose of the control and it is the only purpose.
The only basis of any control in the department is to regulate supply. When the article gets in ample supply the control is lifted. We have lifted a great number of controls in the past three or four months. We have taken the control off practically all steel items and many of the metals. I believe there are only three metals to-day that are controlled. I could go through a long list of items, where controls have been relaxed to some extent. We are not in sufficient supply to be able to remove all of them, but they are coming off as fast as the supply situation will allow. Supply is the only thing that receives consideration in the question whether an article shall be controlled or not, and when the supply situation is easy we take off the control.

Who comprise the War
Assets Corporation?

Just a moment. The question was asked, what does the government intend to do with the air schools? I have covered that. My hon. friend spoke of obsolete armoured vehicles overseas. I am not aware of any; none has been declared surplus to us. My hon. friend will understand that we are the contractors for the armed services. If the 
armed services requisition for a certain item we furnish that item; then it passes into the hands of the service, and it is theirs until it is declared surplus. If they declare it surplus it passes back to the department through the disposal branch. I may say that no items overseas have passed back to us, and therefore I assume that none is surplus.
That does not exactly cover the situation. One frequently hears criticism of the fact that piled up along the right of way of the railways are large amounts of supplies.
I was referring to my hon. friend's remarks about overseas.
I did not refer to overseas.
I thought the hon. member did.
No.

I might explain about the piles along the railways. Materials such as motor trucks and some other items move overseas in very large volume, and they move from a number of ports. For example, there may be coming into New York boats that have considerable surplus space which may be made available for Canadian equipment. They may come to Philadelphia or Baltimore, or on the Canadian side they may come to Halifax, or they may come to Saint John, or in the summer time they may come to one of the ports on the St. Lawrence river. To take advantage of that space-and space is very difficult to come by, and all of those concerned with shipping are very anxious that no boat shall go out without a full load-it is necessary to have a stock-pile of material. Experience has shown that that stock-pile should cover six weeks' output of the store. If it gets down to a month we are certain that boats will go without a full load; therefore we try to keep not less than one month's supply and not more than two months' supply, averaging, as I say, about six weeks' supply in locations where it is readily available for shipment to any one of a number of ports. These stock-piles go up and down. There was a time several months ago when we had practically no stock-piles. The boat situation was easy and we cleaned out practically everything that we had. But ordinarily goods move out of stock-piles and other goods move into stock-piles.
My hon. friend has asked me what goods were in stock-piles three years and what goods were there two years. I can assure him that stock-piles are nbt operated in that way. The first goods in are the first goods out; and while the stock-pile may be there larger or

War Appropriation-Supplies
smaller as he passes through from time to time, the items in that stock-pile are not the items that he saw there five or six months ago. They may look the same externally, because all motorcars are boxed in pretty much the same way and all tires and wheels for motorcars look alike. However, I can assure him that these stock-piles are carefully operated by the controller of transport and his staff; every item in them is listed, and care is taken to see that no items in the stock-piles remain there for any considerable period. That is a necessary feature of the transport of munitions overseas. It is carefully operated. I can asure my hon. friend that the spoilage is surprisingly small. I do not think it is any more than the spoilage that takes place in handling vehicles at any point. Of course, there is a certain amount in loading at the seaboard, and there is a certain amount of spoilage in landing at the other end. But I know something about the spoilage of materials in dumps because these bills come back to the department. I can assure my hon,. friend that they are very much smaller than I anticipated they would be when it was found that it was necessary to have recourse to stock-piles in order to take care of the shipping situation. Does that finish the question?
I asked the minister about two types of material, the quads and the Heath Robinson lorries.

I can assure my hon. friend that everything that has been furnished has been used so far as I know; at least, we have had no rejections. I do not recall the two types. We make only one type of lorry that we call a lorry. It is made by the Chrysler Corporation, and all I can say is that we are making them and the army seems to be accepting them. They are going overseas. That is all I can tell him about that. I do not recall the quad vehicles, but I shall be glad to look the matter up and see if we are making anything in that connection.
The minister mentioned spoilage. Has he any idea of the percentage of the spoilage? What articles are spoiled more than others?
It is not exactly spoilage. It does not spoil. If you drop a box on one corner when you are loading you are likely to spoil the box.
That is damage in transit. When he spoke of spoilage I thought he had in mind articles that are destroyed by weathering in those dumps.

No, none of that, not while it is in our possession. It passes out of our possession at the seaport. I do not know what happens after that. We have had no claims for spoilage of that kind. We have had the odd breakage, of course, but very little of that.

In conclusion, I wish to thank the minister for his explanation of the activities of the Crown Assets Corporation. He has told the committee and the country that the activities of this corporation will be open to parliament. Does he give parliament the assurance that the members of the house will be given such information as they ask in respect of the activities of the corporation regarding the disposal of surpluses or any other disposal that they may make? That is the one point, Mr. Chairman, that I make in connection withi the adoption of the fishbowl principle; that parliament shall have the right to the information. That is of the essence of the whole thing. What I am trying to secure from the minister-and he has been very frank in his explanations-is this: Is parliament to receive the information of the activities of this corporation once it begins to function, or is it to be denied that information?

The present order in council provides that frequent reports shall be made to parliament, and they will be detailed reports. The hon. gentleman asks if members of parliament will be permitted to come in and interfere with the transactions. Of course not.	.
No, no.
After the transaction is made, the House of Commons will be entitled to full details of the transaction.

Is it not true that order in council 9108 provides that the minister shall submit to parliament, within fifteen days of the commencement of the session, a report on the operations of the allocation committee and the company which is set up? [DOT]

I submitted a report in due course and said that no transaction had taken place. My hon. friend will notice I did that. However, legislation will come forward. This is a temporary measure. There was an immediate situation to take care of. Surpluses were arising in munition plants with cancellation of contracts. We wanted to get the procedure going. We are all feeling our way a bit in this, and I had hoped that before this parliament concluded its work we would bring in a bill which we could support with
War Appropriation-Supplies

some experience and perhaps give hon. members a better idea and perhaps have a clearer thought ourselves as to just what the proceeding should be. I think the better place to discuss the disposal company is on the bill that will be introduced into the house this session, instead, of attempting to do so on my estimates. I shall certainly be better briefed at that time.

I have a good deal to say with regard to the war allocations committee.
I am not going to do so now because it is rather late. However, I should like to make this observation for the benefit of the minister. This group are definitely interested in the war allocations committee and the Crown Assets Corporation for perhaps a different reason from that of the hon. member for . Lake Centre.
There is one thing I am convinced of with regard to our post-war plans. If we are to take care of the boys that some of our friends are so vocal in talking about, when they return after the conflict is over, then our postwar plans will largely depend on that corporation as to whether there is to be employment in this country for those who return. In that, connection, when there is time there are some pertinent questions I wish to ask with respect :o the disposal of plants and equipment under *hat set-up.
Progress reported.
